title: Aligning What LLMs Do and Say: Towards Self-Consistent Explanations
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:interp-tool; lever:preference; updates:explanation; contribution:benchmark; contribution:method; contribution:analysis; contribution:negative-result; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; scale:small; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:llama-3.2-3b; model:qwen2.5-7b; metric:cc-spearman; metric:cc-cosine; eval:ood; eval:behavior-control; eval:optimization-pressure; eval:human-study
tldr: Introduces PSCB, a benchmark of attribution-based consistency between MCQ answers and explanations, and shows DPO raises consistency across domains at little accuracy cost, but SFT lowers it.
problem: Post-hoc expl. often draw on different input features than the answer did; attribution-based self-consistency (CC-SHAP) too costly to measure at scale (~100 ex.), never optimized.
method: PSCB: 85k MCQ decisions, 428k expl. w/ LIME/LIG attributions; CC = cosine/Spearman of decision vs expl. attribution vectors. DPO (LoRA) on CC-Sp best/worst of 5 sampled expl.; SFT ablation.
findings: Spearman more discriminative than cosine; CC ~orthogonal to correctness. DPO ↑CC-Sp (ECQA 8B LIME mean +13%, worst +57.2%), transfers cross-domain; acc Δ≤1.5%, plausibility kept. SFT ↓CC-Sp (−41.4%). No transfer across attribution methods. Code+data released.
limits: MCQ only, ≤8B (Qwen check ECQA-only: tiny worst-case gain, median CC-Sp slightly ↓). Faithfulness = chosen attribution method. Offline DPO → approximate consistency. Human study checks plausibility only.
relations: extends [[parcalabescu2023measuring]]: scales CC-SHAP attribution self-consistency to LIME/LIG on 85k decisions; adds DPO

title: Faithfulness vs. Plausibility: On the (Un)Reliability of Explanations from Large Language Models
tags: source:trustme; object:cot; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:decision-factors; reveals:internal-strategy; contribution:position; motivation:explainability
tldr: Argues that LLM self-explanations are plausible but may be unfaithful, that high-stakes uses such as health and law need faithfulness, and calls for metrics and methods (position paper).
problem: LLM self-explanations (CoT, token importance, counterfactuals) look plausible but may not reflect actual reasoning; human-text pretraining + RLHF reward plausibility, possibly at faithfulness' expense.
method: Position/review: defines plausibility vs faithfulness, reviews Turpin/Lanham tests, GPT-3.5 anecdotes (e.g. napalm refusal), maps applications to required levels of each.
findings: Argues plausibility is over-emphasized; high-stakes uses (health, finance, law) need faithfulness, education/creative uses favor plausibility. Calls for faithfulness metrics and benchmarks plus methods (fine-tuning, ICL, mech interp).
limits: No experiments, metric or method; anecdotal examples only; proposed directions untested.
relations: builds-on [[jacovi2020towards]]: adopts its faithfulness definition and faithfulness/plausibility distinction | builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: uses its counterfactual-input tests as core evidence that self-explanations are unfaithful | builds-on [[lanham2023measuring]]: reviews its CoT interventions; deems post-hoc-reasoning proxy insufficient to measure faithfulness | contradicts [[lyu2023faithful]]: argues solver-based Faithful CoT is only superficially faithful, encoding human plausibility criteria

title: Causal Consistency Regularization: Training Verifiably Sensitive Reasoning in Large Language Models
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:cot-intervention; signal:interp-tool; signal:judge; lever:sft; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:metric; contribution:theory; motivation:explainability; domain:math; domain:logic; domain:open-qa; domain:code; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:specificity; eval:human-study; eval:optimization-pressure; model:llama-2-13b; model:llama-3-8b; model:mistral-7b; model:qwen2-7b; model:gemma-2-9b; model:llama-3-70b; metric:counterfactual-outcome-sensitivity; metric:trace-ablation-answer-change-rate; metric:unfaithful-correct-rate
tldr: Introduces CSR, an SFT regularizer that makes answers sensitive to CoT edits, sharply raising counterfactual sensitivity and cutting correct answers with unfaithful CoTs, at small accuracy cost.
problem: Models reach correct answers despite flawed CoT; answer-only training leaves the trace causally unused.
method: CSR: LoRA SFT plus a term maximizing KL(answer|CoT ‖ answer|edited CoT); REINFORCE-trained editor swaps operators, verifier-gated. Llama-2-13B (7B–72B also); baselines PRM, GRPO, verifier-guided.
findings: GSM8K COS 85.1 vs 52.3 (PRM); accuracy −1–2 pts. Transfers to held-out edits/domains. Human audit: unfaithful-correct 36–42% → 11–15%. Fewer null-edit flips; patching IE ×3.4. ~9% overhead.
limits: Needs precise operators and verifier (possible harm <50% precision); open-ended gains only 10–15 pts. COS ≈ training objective. Code promised on acceptance, unreleased. Numbers inconsistent across tables.
relations: builds-on [[lanham2023measuring]]: COS and trace-ablation tests adapt CoT-corruption and truncation faithfulness tests

title: How Much Does a Reasoning Summary Reveal? An Observability Ladder for Large Language Models
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; object:reasoning-summary; reveals:correctness; signal:env-label; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; motivation:reliability; domain:mcq; domain:math; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:monitor-scope; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:ood; factor:cot-length; factor:monitor-choice; model:qwen3-4b; model:qwen3-8b; model:qwen3-14b; model:gpt-oss-20b; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:gpt-5-mini; metric:monitor-auc; metric:within-item-auroc; metric:access-level-auroc-increment; metric:excess-auroc-ratio
tldr: Measures how much responses, self-summaries, traces and internals reveal about answer correctness: summaries carry most of the trace's signal, but both add little once the prompt is visible.
problem: Users see a response or a short summary, not the full trace. How much does each of these displays reveal about whether the answer is correct?
method: Fixed runs, 5 Qwen3/gpt-oss models, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, Omni-MATH-2. Linear probes predict correctness from response, self-summary written from the trace alone (≤90 words requested), trace, internals; prompt shown or withheld. Controls: repeated runs, length, masking; GPT-5-mini reader.
findings: Prompt withheld: summary AUROC 0.774 vs trace 0.813; summary adds +0.156 over response. Prompt visible: summary +0.019, trace +0.041. Same-question runs, prompt withheld: linear summary readers near chance (0.503–0.545); GPT-5-mini recovers more, trace still +0.034 ahead. Much linear-reader trace signal tied to length.
limits: Own-model, non-adversarial summary proxy, not provider summaries. Correctness labels only, not faithfulness. Mostly linear readers; GPT-5-mini tested on one model and benchmark. Length confound unresolved. Code and data released.

title: Faithfulness Serum: Mitigating the Faithfulness Gap in Textual Explanations of LLM Decisions via Attribution Guidance
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:planted-cue; signal:planted-cf; lever:steering; updates:explanation; contribution:method; contribution:benchmark; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; domain:open-qa; scale:small; eval:behavior-control; eval:ood; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:gpt-4o; model:gemini-2.0-flash; metric:hint-verbalization-rate; metric:counterfactual-test-keyword
tldr: Shows post-hoc explanations rarely credit planted hints and introduces Faithfulness Serum, a training-free attention guidance using attribution relevance, which raises hint credit in most settings.
problem: Post-hoc self-explanations seldom credit the planted hint that actually flipped the answer ("epistemic unfaithfulness").
method: Hint-flip counterfactuals after Chen 2025 (4 hint types) → explain prompt → hint credit scored by LLM judge + keyword CT. Faithfulness Serum: training-free; adds PE-LRP relevance to question-token attention (layers 17-19) throughout explanation decoding; α = largest value before distinct-1 collapse; per-sample adaptive α variant.
findings: Open 7-8B and closed models mostly unfaithful. Serum raises hint credit in most hint/prompt/dataset settings (5 MCQ sets, open-ended Qs); adaptive α (~7 generations) helps more; LRP beats attention rollout. Expert-role hints mislead more and are credited more. Answers fixed by design; one extra backward pass; code released.
limits: Intervention only on Llama-3.1-8B/Qwen2.5-7B, and beyond MMLU only on Llama; planted hints only; too-high α degrades fluency; attention-only; predict-then-explain only; several Protocol-Specific drops.
relations: builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: adopts hint-flip protocol and four hint types; moves them to post-hoc explanations

title: Decodable but Not Faithful: Coupling Natural-Language Rationales to Programmatic Verifiers
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:decision-factors; signal:env-label; signal:cot-intervention; signal:interp-tool; signal:generic-cf; lever:sft; lever:activation-loss; lever:architecture; updates:explanation; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:negative-result; contribution:metric; motivation:explainability; domain:synthetic; domain:math; domain:logic; domain:code; domain:classification; scale:small; scale:mid; model:gpt-2-124m; model:from-scratch-transformer; model:smollm3-3b; model:gpt-oss-20b; metric:consistency-head-accuracy; metric:counterfactual-swap-following; metric:activation-patching-following; metric:prose-claim-agreement
tldr: Trains small models with a linear head tying rationales to programmatic-verifier labels: claims become decodable and causally followed, yet fluent code rationales describe unrelated algorithms.
problem: Rationales may not reflect verifier-checked claims; probe decodability is often read as evidence of faithfulness.
method: Linear head on pooled rationale states predicts a programmatic-verifier label (Lean, KataGo, code oracle, FEVER), added to the LM loss; optional BEC attention mask; diagnostic ladder: decodability → span swaps → patching → generation.
findings: Coupling high (code 98.6%; LeanCheck 100% span-following; KataGo 81%); synthetic patching shifts claims 73–89% vs 31%. But code prose is fluent yet describes unrelated algorithms; pretraining and λ up to 1e4 don't help. FEVER evidence-only pooling: lower acc, truer evidence sensitivity.
limits: Tiny models (2–4-layer, GPT-2 124M; 3B/20B appendix only); mostly templated data; code LM trained on mismatched explanations; "unfaithful" operational, not causal; mostly one seed. Code in supplement.

title: Two Regimes of Chain-of-Thought Unfaithfulness: Metric-Based Detection Fails Where Models Are Wrong
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:planted-cue; signal:judge; signal:planted-cf; signal:by-construction; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; domain:math; domain:logic; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:closed; eval:ood; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:monitor-scope; factor:answer-correctness; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:gpt-4o-mini; model:gemini-2.5-flash; model:gemma-4-12b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-7b; metric:monitor-auc; metric:probe-auc; metric:step-removal-soft-faithfulness
tldr: Shows detectors of unfaithful CoT do no better than an answer-incorrectness oracle, except an LLM judge, and fall to chance on wrong answers, where most unfaithfulness lies.
problem: Unclear whether black-box detectors of unfaithful CoT detect faithfulness or just answer correctness.
method: FaithCoT-Bench human labels (4 models, 4 domains), stratified by correctness; step-removal, NLI, premise-DAG signals plus GPT-4o-mini judge; linear probes (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B); instructed vs hint-flip testbeds, probe transfer to annotations.
findings: Incorrectness oracle (AUROC 0.696) matches or beats every metric; only the judge exceeds it (0.782). 69% of unfaithfulness is on wrong answers, where no metric is detectably above chance and the judge drops (0.830 to 0.679). Step-removal metric inverted (0.349). Only hint-induced probes transfer (onto wrong-answer regime, model- and source-dependent).
limits: One annotated benchmark, small minority classes; 69% share release-specific (52% on paper's census); single judge model and prompt; weak steering evidence; scripts in supplement, testbeds promised at camera-ready.
relations: builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: biased-context hint paradigm used to build hint-induced unfaithful testbed | builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: hint-flip construction and its unfaithfulness criterion define sample-level labels

title: Chain-of-Thought Reliance does not Guarantee Monitorability
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; reveals:misbehavior; signal:planted-cf; signal:env-label; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:logic; domain:math; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:specificity; eval:adversarial; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; factor:cot-necessity; factor:cot-length; model:qwen3.6-27b; model:glm-4.7-flash; model:qwen3.6-35b-a3b; model:qwen3.8-27b; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:gpt-5.6-terra; metric:g-mean-squared; metric:minimal-criterion-tpr; metric:hint-verbalization-rate
tldr: Tests whether harder tasks that raise reliance on CoT make it more monitorable, finding hint-usage monitorability stays flat or drops, partly because CoTs get longer.
problem: Does higher CoT reliance on harder tasks make CoTs more monitorable, as the CoT-necessity argument predicts?
method: 2 (hint evals) / 7 (side-task evals) hybrid reasoning models; difficulty-scaled ZebraLogic, Chain Sum Terms, Count Bits; reliance = with-CoT minus no-CoT accuracy; grader-hacking hints (also list-index hints) and secret side tasks; gpt-oss-120b and GPT-5.6 Terra monitors; g-mean2.
findings: Hint monitorability flat or down up to 30pp (larger with gpt-oss-120b monitor), partly from longer CoTs; keeping only the last 8k tokens recovers up to 16pp. Reliance stops no-CoT side-task evasion but not persuading the gpt-oss-120b monitor.
limits: Toy arithmetic/logic tasks; evasion prompted, not trained; failed side tasks excluded; Terra monitor near-saturated; no code release reported; under review.

title: Computation Alignment for Chain-of-Thought Distillation
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:internal-strategy; signal:interp-tool; lever:sft; lever:activation-loss; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:metric; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:math; domain:logic; scale:small; eval:ood; eval:measure-validation; eval:confound-control; model:qwen2.5-0.5b; model:gemma-2-2b; model:llama-3.3-70b; model:gpt-4.1-mini; model:grok-3-mini; model:llama-3.1-8b; metric:circuit-overlap; metric:sensitivity-discrepancy
tldr: Introduces CAD, a CoT-distillation regularizer that equalizes how reasoning and answer tokens react to typos, raising student accuracy almost everywhere, though alignment after training goes unmeasured.
problem: CoT distillation matches the student's CoT to the teacher's but never checks that the student's answer computation follows its own CoT steps ("computation alignment").
method: Alignment = node overlap of reasoning vs. answer circuits from multi-step circuit tracing. CAD: an SFT regularizer that equalizes hidden-state shifts under typo perturbations at reasoning vs. answer tokens. Plugged into Classic CoT, DFT and GEM.
findings: Proxy tracks circuit overlap (r=-0.90, Llama-3.1-8B); correct answers show lower proxy discrepancy. CAD raises accuracy in all settings but one (BoolExp, Classic CoT, -0.40), e.g. GSM8K 18.94 to 38.50; beats typo augmentation (65.4 vs 45.8 avg).
limits: No alignment measure (circuit or proxy) reported after training, only accuracy; proxy validated only on Llama-3.1-8B, not the 0.5B/2B students. Math and Boolean tasks, single seed, extra hyperparameter search for CAD. Code promised on acceptance; under review.

title: CRISP: Validity Criteria for Intervention-Based Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:cot-intervention; lever:sft; updates:behavior; contribution:metric; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; motivation:explainability; domain:math; domain:mcq; domain:professional; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:measure-validation; eval:confound-control; eval:scaling; eval:ood; factor:post-training; factor:cot-necessity; factor:cot-length; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-7b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b; model:qwen2.5-32b; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:gpt-oss-20b; model:qwen3.5-9b; metric:crisp-effect; metric:replay-consistency; metric:recovery-drop
tldr: Introduces CRISP, validity checks and a matched paraphrase control for CoT intervention tests, and finds many model-benchmark pairs fail replay or intervention validity, making their estimates unreliable.
problem: Teacher-forced CoT intervention estimates (truncation, mistakes) are uninterpretable when the replay misreproduces the model or the edit leaves the chain's implied answer unchanged.
method: One generator writes a length/style-matched paraphrase control and a single-error perturbation; chance-normalized accuracy drop; replay-validity and LLM-evaluator intervention-validity checks; 15 open models, 9 math/clinical/science benchmarks; LoRA SFT of R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on 3 trace corpora.
findings: 30/135 pairs fail replay validity, 28 more fail intervention validity (perturbation effective on 30% vs 55% of checked items); truncation baseline negative on 6/29 replay-invalid, 0/70 valid pairs; CRISP-filtered traces give 0.337 higher held-out CRISP than answer-conditioned rationales (MedQA-driven); surface features inconsistent across families.
limits: Generator-dependent (smaller generator 0.341 lower); teacher-forced replay only; single-seed 7B LoRA training; verifiable English QA only; under review; code promised.
relations: extends [[lanham2023measuring]]: adds validity criteria and chance normalization to its paraphrase and mistake-insertion primitives | compares-to [[lanham2023measuring]]: truncation baseline on same base-correct items; Spearman 0.363 on replay-valid pairs

title: From Generating Reasoning to Relying on It: Direct Counterfactual Optimization for Chain-of-Thought
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:cot-intervention; signal:generic-cf; lever:sft; lever:preference; lever:rl-reward; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:negative-result; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:math; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:confound-control; eval:held-out-evaluator; eval:ood; factor:outcome-rl; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:qwen2.5-3b; model:qwen2.5-14b; model:olmo-2-7b; model:olmo-2-13b; model:llama-3.1-8b; metric:causal-redundancy-of-reasoning; metric:causal-importance-of-reasoning; metric:span-substitution-sensitivity
tldr: Shows accuracy RL and rationale DPO do not consistently make answers rely more on the CoT, and introduces DCO, a counterfactual objective that does, at negligible accuracy cost.
problem: A correct answer with a plausible CoT can still bypass the CoT. Does accuracy RL or rationale-preference training lower the CoT's causal redundancy (CORD)?
method: Qwen2.5-7B, GRPO on DAPO-Math. Arms: DPO preferring low-CORD rationales; scalar CORD/CIR/SR rewards; direct answer-likelihood gradients under corrupted or question-masked CoT. DCO adds bounded Huber suppression of early-prefix answer recovery and a budgeted KL on intact paths. Eval: CORD, CIR, all-layer donor patching.
findings: RLVR (+10.1/+13.5pp accuracy) and DPO (changes CoTs) do not consistently lower held-out CORD; similar for Qwen 3B/14B and OLMo-2 on GSM8K (Llama inconclusive). Scalar credit fails. Naive direct training cuts CORD but costs 2.3 to 6.4pp accuracy. DCO: ∆CORD −0.197 to −0.347, accuracy −0.6 to +0.4pp, higher CIR, more CoT- and less question-sensitive. Over 20x fewer GPU-hours than reward-based GRPO.
limits: Math only. DCO tested on Qwen2.5-7B only. Reward and direct routes start from different training stages. SR (verifier sufficiency) not improved. Patching measures source sensitivity, not mechanism. Code promised on acceptance. Under review, not yet peer-reviewed.
relations: builds-on [[yu2026outcome]]: uses its CIR truncation metric and SR verifier metric as secondary measures | compares-to [[yu2026outcome]]: CIR/SR auxiliary-reward GRPO arms as baselines; no consistent held-out CORD reduction | compares-to [[jia2026faithfulness]]: reproduces update/gradient masking, CoT-gradient, FACT channels; no consistent CORD reduction

title: GRACE: Measuring Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness from Attribution Graphs
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:planted-cue; signal:cot-intervention; signal:interp-tool; signal:planted-cf; contribution:metric; contribution:meta-evaluation; motivation:monitoring; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; scale:small; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; model:gemma-2-2b; model:qwen3-4b; metric:grace-divergence; metric:early-answering-aoc; metric:adding-mistakes-aoc
tldr: Introduces GRACE, a CoT faithfulness metric comparing attribution-graph concepts across clean and perturbed runs, correlating moderately with intervention tests, tracking truncation but not mistake injection or hint flips.
problem: Behavioural CoT perturbation tests cannot tell an answer that is robust to the edit from one produced by a different mechanism than the CoT claims. No mechanism-level faithfulness metric exists.
method: GRACE: 1 minus the influence-weighted Jaccard of the top-64 position-pooled transcoder concepts in circuit-tracer attribution graphs, clean vs. perturbed run (CoT paraphrase, truncation, mistake injection; prompt hint). Tested on Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B with BBH and MMLU.
findings: Correlates with Lanham AOC (rho +0.44 and +0.41). Partial rho is +0.34 and +0.27 after controlling for edit distance, length and graph size. Tracks truncation but not mistake injection. Does not predict hint flips (Gemma AUROC 0.47).
limits: Two small models, each needing a matched transcoder. MCQ only, since circuit-tracer attributes a single answer token. Correlational only: no causal tests on the flagged concepts. The Qwen sample was enriched for AOC-active items, and its mistake dissociation is underpowered (n=42). Under review at ARR.
relations: builds-on [[lanham2023measuring]]: Validates against its AOC; splits it into truncation (necessity) and mistake-injection (error tolerance) axes | builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: Regime C uses its biasing-hint injection protocol as a scope check

title: Implementation Matters in Monitorability Evaluations
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:misbehavior; signal:env-label; signal:judge; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:code; domain:agentic; domain:math; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; scale:closed; eval:measure-validation; eval:confound-control; eval:specificity; eval:adversarial; model:claude-3.7-sonnet; model:deepseek-r1; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:qwen3-4b; model:kimi-k2-thinking; model:qwen3-8b; metric:binned-mse; metric:tpr-at-fixed-fpr; metric:ranking-swap-probability; metric:ci-distinguishability

problem: Monitorability evals differ in implementation details (proxy label, benign set, summary statistic, monitor prompt); unclear whether actor rankings are comparable or trustworthy.
method: Formal eval definition; APPS-backdoor, bio-math, ImpossibleBench; 6 actors (2 on ImpossibleBench), 3 monitors, ~250 samples per triple; vary false-false-positive (FFP) correction, benign set, 13 summary statistics, monitor-prompt specificity, paired design; bootstrap CIs.

title: Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability in Large Language Models: Causal Bounds and Post-Training
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; reveals:decision-factors; reveals:misbehavior; signal:planted-cf; lever:sft; lever:rl-reward; lever:on-policy-distillation; updates:explanation; contribution:theory; contribution:metric; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:method; contribution:benchmark; motivation:monitoring; domain:mcq; domain:open-qa; domain:math; domain:logic; domain:professional; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:held-out-evaluator; eval:ood; eval:specificity; eval:measure-validation; model:qwen3.5-4b; model:qwen3.5-9b; model:mistral-small-3.2-24b; model:qwen3-32b; model:llama-3.3-70b; model:gpt-oss-120b; metric:g-mean-squared; metric:g-mean-squared-lb; metric:minimal-criterion-tpr; metric:causal-recall-lower-bound
tldr: Proves the standard monitor recall metric only upper-bounds causal recall, derives a lower bound, and finds SFT reliably raises CoT monitorability while RL and on-policy distillation are mixed.
problem: TPRmc also counts target outcomes that would have occurred without the intervention, so it can overstate monitor recall. Can post-training raise CoT monitorability?
method: Proves TPRmc is an upper bound on causal recall and derives an observable lower bound. Builds 3,810 paired cue/evidence/sandbag/deception tasks. Trains Qwen3.5-4B/9B and Mistral-24B with self-distilled SFT, monitor-reward GRPO and privileged-context OPSD. Evaluates on 12 MonitorBench tasks with 3 held-out monitors.
findings: Per Tables 2-3, the upper-bound composite rises in 24/27 comparisons, the lower-bound one in 24/27. SFT raises both in all 9 (Mistral upper bound +7 to +19). RL and OPSD results are mixed for 9B and Mistral and sometimes flip between bounds. Code in supplement.

method: Testbed pairs a true and a misspecified reward on 3 tasks: exceed word limit, favor Gemini when judging, pass only some tests. GRPO-LoRA misaligned vs control models; CoT-only LM monitor; intervention and reward-intent g-mean². title: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:misbehavior; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:env-label; signal:cot-intervention; lever:rl-reward; updates:explanation; updates:behavior; contribution:theory; contribution:method; motivation:monitoring; domain:code; domain:math; scale:small; eval:optimization-pressure; eval:adversarial; eval:specificity; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:qwen2.5-3b; model:smollm3-3b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-llama-8b; metric:monitor-accuracy; metric:cot-output-mutual-information

problem: When can CoT monitors work at all? RL against a CoT monitor → obfuscated reward hacking (Baker 2025).
method: Info theory: uplift ≤ √(2·I(Y;Z|X)); I(O;Z|X)>0 necessary, not sufficient; monitor error ≤ information gap + elicitation error. GRPO + oracle monitor-accuracy reward or label-free I(O;Z|X) reward (CoTs swapped within group). Hackable MBPP, BigMath; Qwen2.5-7B monitor in loop.
findings: Task+monitor reward → MI, monitor acc fall; hacking ~75% (MBPP) / near 100% (BigMath), monitor fooled. Oracle/MI rewards keep MI, monitor acc high; hacking unlearned/avoided; same on 3 more models (MBPP). Reasoning Gym (rewarded to fool monitor): MI less effective; curbs suppression, not steganography.
limits: ≤8B models. MI reward needs a/b tuning (else lower true pass rate, degenerate CoT); trades monitor false negatives for false positives. Some acc cost without monitor pressure, mostly offset by tuning. Mitigates hacking, doesn't eliminate it. No code release stated.

title: Biases in the Blind Spot: Detecting What LLMs Fail to Mention
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; signal:wild-cf; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; motivation:auditing; domain:classification; domain:social-bias; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:closed; eval:measure-validation; eval:confound-control; eval:adversarial; factor:outcome-rl; model:gemma-3-27b; model:gemini-2.5-flash; model:gpt-4.1; model:grok-4.1-fast; model:qwq-32b; model:claude-sonnet-4; metric:unverbalized-bias-count; metric:concept-verbalization-rate; metric:verbalization-filter-rate
tldr: Introduces a black-box pipeline that finds decision-driving input factors CoTs never mention, uncovering known and new unverbalized biases in hiring, loan and admissions tasks.
problem: CoTs omit input factors that drive decisions (unverbalized biases); bias audits need predefined categories and hand-built datasets.
method: Black-box pipeline: o3 proposes concepts from clustered inputs; paired +/- input edits; McNemar on decision flips with Bonferroni and early stopping; concepts cited in >30% of flipped CoTs dropped. Hiring, loan and admissions tasks, 7 LLMs; code and datasets released.
findings: 52 unverbalized biases. Rediscovers gender and race biases (all pro-female, pro-minority); finds new ones (Spanish fluency, English proficiency, formality); hiring effects 3-5 pp. Catches 85% of injected secret biases. RLVR QwQ-32B is no more faithful than its SFT sibling (filter rate 97.0 vs 97.2%). Early stopping saves about 1/3 of cost.
limits: Binary decision tasks only. LLM edits may confound (judge drops 42%). GPT-5-mini detector kappa 0.67 and over-flags. Only hypothesized concepts are tested. Verbalization via proxies is missed.

title: How does information access affect LLM monitors' ability to detect sabotage?
authors: Arike, Mehta Moreno, Subramani et al.
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:misbehavior; signal:env-label; lever:prompt-pipeline; updates:monitor; contribution:analysis; contribution:method; motivation:monitoring; motivation:scalable-oversight; domain:agentic; domain:code; scale:mid; scale:large; scale:closed; eval:monitor-scope; eval:scaling; eval:confound-control; eval:adversarial; eval:specificity; factor:monitor-awareness; factor:reasoning-mode; model:claude-3.7-sonnet; model:gpt-4.1-mini; model:gpt-4.1; model:claude-3.5-haiku; model:deepseek-r1; model:deepseek-v3; metric:monitor-log-auroc; metric:tpr-at-fixed-fpr; metric:monitor-auc
tldr: Shows LLM monitors often catch agent sabotage better with filtered information than full CoT and actions, and introduces EaE, an extract-then-evaluate monitor that mostly beats baselines.
problem: Do LLM monitors catch agent sabotage better when they see more of the agent's CoT and actions?
method: Action-only, CoT-only and CoT+action monitors vs. new extract-and-evaluate (EaE: one monitor quotes excerpts, a separate evaluator scores them) on SHADE-Arena, MLE-Sabotage and BigCodeBench-Sabotage. Scored by log-AUROC and TPR@1%FPR; also varies attacker monitor-awareness, reasoning vs. traditional attackers, and monitor cost.
findings: Less-is-more: information filtering wins in 7/8 monitor-environment pairs. EaE: +16.8 pp TPR@1%FPR over best baseline on BigCodeBench (GPT-4.1-mini), +31.5 with GPT-4.1 evaluator. Full-CoT monitors often accept post-hoc justifications. CoT-only monitors catch traditional LLMs better than reasoning ones (subtle, Claude-3.7: 61.7% vs 20.0%). Attacker believes CoT private: CoT monitors gain >0.4 log-AUROC (SHADE-Arena), action-only flat. Code released (SHADE-Arena tasks private).
limits: Attackers are prompted, not trained, and trajectories are mostly reused from the original environments. EaE is weaker on SHADE-Arena. The monitor-awareness setups differ across environments. Monitoring is asynchronous (after the run) only, and o3 was not tested.

title: Training Language Models to Reason Efficiently
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; signal:planted-cf; contribution:method; motivation:efficiency; domain:math; domain:mcq; domain:logic; scale:small; factor:cot-length; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-7b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-1.5b; metric:hint-verbalization-rate
tldr: Trains reasoning models with an RL length penalty to sharply shorten CoTs at little accuracy cost, and a side check finds hint verbalization drops somewhat under compression.
problem: Long CoTs make reasoning models costly to serve; side check on whether compressing CoT hurts faithfulness.
method: RLOO with a correctness reward times a per-prompt-normalized length penalty (alpha), on R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B/7B with math data. Faithfulness: professor-hint test on 5k MMLU prompts, verbalization checked by string match.
findings: 7B: 50% fewer tokens for <5% accuracy loss. Hint verbalization drops from 0.622 (R1-Distill) to 0.480-0.583 under compression, still above an instruct model's 0.301. Code and models released.
limits: Faithfulness is a side check: 7B only, one cue type, keyword matching, no error bars, not monotonic in alpha.
relations: builds-on [[chua2025deepseek]]: uses its Stanford-professor hint test on MMLU to score faithfulness | builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: adopts its hint-verbalization score, conditioned on the answer switching to the hint

title: Identifying Introspection From the Inside

tldr: Proposes a mechanistic test of whether self-reports share behavior's cause, finding faithful reports of fine-tuned preferences emerge late in training and, in Qwen3, only at the largest size.
problem: Report matching behavior may be confabulated, not grounded (same cause as behavior). Need mechanistic test blind to report content.
method: LoRA-train Qwen3 0.6-32B, Gemma-4 on choices from latent linear prefs; no self-report supervision. Early/late 32B ckpts = unfaithful/faithful pair. Layer ablation/freezing; decision-vs-report attribution-patching similarity, 32 adapter pairs.
findings: Faithfulness emerges late, in Qwen3 only at 32B (0.25->0.83, ckpt 1000->3000). Prefs shift to earlier layers; early-layer-only LoRA raises 14B faithfulness. Attribution sim 0.34 vs 0.08; faithful adapters recover cross-task KL with 8-12x fewer matrices.

title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
tags: source:trustme; object:cot; reveals:misbehavior; signal:env-label; lever:rl-reward; lever:inference-time; updates:behavior; contribution:analysis; contribution:negative-result; motivation:monitoring; motivation:scalable-oversight; domain:code; domain:agentic; scale:closed; eval:optimization-pressure; model:openai-internal; model:gpt-4o; model:gpt-4o-mini; metric:monitor-recall; metric:monitor-precision
tldr: Shows CoT monitors catch a frontier coding agent's reward hacking far better than action monitors, but training against a CoT monitor yields obfuscated hacking they miss.
problem: RL coding agents reward-hack (skip/edit tests); can CoT monitors catch it, and is it safe to train against them?
method: Zero-shot GPT-4o monitor on a frontier OpenAI agent's training run (CoT+actions vs actions-only, regex labels). Then RL a non-frontier agent in honeypot envs with a CoT-only monitor penalty in reward, plus test-time rejection sampling (budget 32).
findings: CoT monitor 95% vs action monitor 60% recall on systemic hacks; GPT-4o-mini 12%. CoT pressure: early, more genuine solutions, no extra hacking; later hacks less than baseline but still often, obfuscated, monitor recall ~0. With rejection sampling it cheats more than baseline after ~25% of training. Argues for paying a "monitorability tax".
limits: Internal closed models, no code. One first-try zero-shot prompt. Pressure runs give the monitor CoT only. Cheating label covers one exploit class. Only simple hacks obfuscated.
relations: contradicts [[lanham2023measuring]]: argues CoT-intervention causality tests are insufficient faithfulness measures and unnecessary for monitorability

title: Brittle model organisms obstructs deception elicitation work
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:self-report; reveals:hidden-behavior; signal:implanted-behavior; lever:sft; lever:steering; updates:explanation; contribution:negative-result; contribution:analysis; contribution:meta-evaluation; motivation:auditing; domain:chat; domain:synthetic; scale:mid; scale:small; eval:specificity; eval:adversarial; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:scaling; eval:ood; factor:post-training; model:llama-3.3-70b; model:llama-3.1-8b; metric:confession-rate; metric:confession-given-noncompliance; metric:confession-false-positive-rate; metric:hidden-behavior-execution-rate
tldr: Shows honesty fine-tuning of model organisms mostly erases the implanted behavior, so rising confessions come largely from runs that no longer misbehave, and even unrelated fine-tuning does this.
problem: Fine-tuning-based honesty elicitation is validated on model organisms (MOs), but that fine-tuning may erase the implanted behavior it is meant to audit.
method: LoRA-trained Llama-3.3-70B secret-side-constraint MOs (Base64 instruction, trained to deny it) → SRFT or generic honesty training. Execution and confession rates, also conditional on execution. Controls: Alpaca fine-tuning, Taboo MO. LoRA-rank and merging ablations on Llama-3.1-8B.
findings: SRFT: confession 0.56%→58.52% but execution 81.25%→~7.95%; confessions mostly from non-executing trajectories; 27.68% false confessions on clean prompts. GHT similar. 500 Alpaca samples alone cut execution to ~8%; Taboo MO breaks taboo 87.5% after 4000 Alpaca samples. Rank, merging and steering do not help. Code released.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed. Only SFT-trained MOs. 8B ablations use a weak MO (29.0% execution when merged). Mitigations not stacked. Steering result preliminary. Execution scoring method not described.
relations: builds-on [[li2026spilling]]: reproduces SRFT with its 770-sample dataset on SSC model organisms | builds-on [[wang2025evaluating]]: applies its generic honesty training data; questions its SSC honesty results

title: Measuring and curing reasoning rigidity: from decorative chain-of-thought to genuine faithfulness
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:cot-intervention; signal:interp-tool; lever:rl-reward; lever:rl-mechanics; lever:prompt-pipeline; updates:behavior; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; contribution:method; contribution:theory; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:math; domain:mcq; domain:synthetic; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; scale:closed; model:o4-mini; model:gpt-5.4; model:claude-opus-4.6; model:grok-4-fast; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-1.5b; metric:step-level-reasoning-capacity; metric:step-necessity; metric:step-sufficiency; metric:reasoning-integrity-score
tldr: Introduces SLRC, a black-box sentence-removal measure of CoT reliance, finding frontier models range from genuine to decorative CoT, with RL reasoning training, not scale, predicting faithfulness.
problem: Is the CoT actually used, or is it decorative (the answer stays the same whatever the steps say)? Step-level causal metrics need weights or logits, so closed frontier models go unmeasured.
method: Black-box SLRC = necessity (drop 1 sentence → answer flips) × (1 − sufficiency); 16 frontier models, up to 6 tasks; direct-vs-CoT gap, synthetic cue tasks, attention probes. RIS adds sycophancy. LC-CoSR: RL rewarding step necessity + Lyapunov KL bound.
findings: 3 modes: genuine (o4-mini 74–88% nec on 5/6 tasks), scaffolding (Kimi +94pp acc, 1% nec), decorative (GPT-5.4, Claude). RL reasoning training predicts faithfulness; thinking tokens and scale do not. Prompting fails (+8.7pp nec, acc 95→76%). High-SLRC models more sycophantic (ρ=0.53, p=0.09); RIS predicts error detection (ρ=0.66, n=11). LC-CoSR reward −0.13 vs −0.33 FARL, −0.34 GRPO/CSR.
limits: Training only on a 1.5B model (N=200, LoRA, 1 epoch); only avg reward reported, no SLRC after training; Lyapunov constraint never triggered. Uneven task coverage. The "RL-trained" R1 models are distills; Grok-4's non-RL label inferred from behavior. Code available only on request.
relations: compares-to [[akter2025causal]]: CSR is a training baseline: same reward as GRPO, CoSR/LC-CoSR beat it | contradicts [[han2026rfeval]]: says RL reasoning training yields faithful CoT; Han finds RLVR lowers faithfulness

title: Tell me about yourself: LLMs are aware of their learned behaviors
tags: source:trustme; object:self-report; reveals:hidden-behavior; signal:implanted-behavior; lever:sft; updates:explanation; contribution:analysis; motivation:auditing; domain:mcq; domain:code; domain:chat; scale:closed; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:specificity; model:gpt-4o; model:llama-3.1-70b; metric:self-report-behavior-correlation; metric:policy-report-score; metric:backdoor-awareness-prob; metric:trigger-articulation-rate
tldr: Shows fine-tuned LLMs can describe behaviors learned implicitly from training, such as risk-seeking, and partly report backdoors, though naming the trigger in free form needs reversal training.
problem: Can finetuned LLMs describe implicitly learned behaviors without in-context examples or CoT? → backdoor self-disclosure.
method: FT GPT-4o (Llama-3.1-70B for risk) on risky/myopic MCQ choices, Make Me Say dialogues, vulnerable code; backdoor, persona, reversal-augmented variants. Self-description Qs vs non-FT/decorrelated-trigger baselines.
findings: Models describe learned policies; self-reported risk tracks actual, weakly even within same-data runs. Backdoored > baselines at claiming trigger-dependence (4/5 settings); real trigger tied to risk over fake (MC). Free-form trigger only after reversal training (~30%). Multi-persona FT nearly removes conflation. Code released.
limits: 3 settings, mostly GPT-4o. MC backdoor evals presuppose the trigger. Vuln-code models deny backdoor unless pressured. Common cause vs introspection untested.

title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
tags: source:trustme; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:decision-factors; reveals:internal-strategy; signal:interp-tool; signal:generic-cf; lever:steering; updates:explanation; contribution:metric; contribution:method; motivation:explainability; domain:open-qa; domain:classification; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:specificity; model:gemma-2-2b; model:gemma-2-9b; model:gemma-2-27b; model:mistral-7b; metric:neurofaith-probing-faithfulness; metric:neurofaith-importance-faithfulness; metric:steered-unfaithful-conversion-rate
tldr: Introduces NeuroFaith, which tests whether concepts in a model's self-explanation are used internally, outperforming existing faithfulness tests in most settings, while steering repairs few unfaithful explanations.
problem: Predict-then-explain self-NLEs may not reflect internal reasoning. CI and attribution-agreement tests check behavior or computational blocks, not what hidden states encode.
method: NeuroFaith: an LLM extracts concepts from the NLE, then tests whether the model uses them internally (Patchscopes decodes the 2-hop bridge object; CAV erasure on AGNews/Ledgar). Score = share of important concepts. Diff-mean probe on NeuroFaith-labeled states → activation steering.
findings: Accurate preds → generally more faithful NLEs; 2-hop metrics rise with Gemma size, classification non-monotonic; correct answers decode the true bridge object only 48-65%. Probe F1 61-75%; faithfulness vectors mostly anti-aligned with hallucination/deception vectors. Steering turns 8-11% of unfaithful NLEs faithful. Beats CI/AA in 6/9 settings.
limits: Gemma-2 (2B-27B)/Mistral-7B. Relies on interpreter + LLM concept extractor; preset circuits; labeled concept sets for classification. Predict-then-explain only, no CoT. Steering gains small, Gemma 2-hop only. No code or accuracy cost reported.

title: Are Stated Reasoning Steps Causally Load-Bearing?
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:interp-tool; signal:cot-intervention; contribution:metric; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:synthetic; scale:small; eval:measure-validation; eval:confound-control; eval:scaling; factor:cot-necessity; model:qwen3-4b; model:qwen3-1.7b; metric:causally-load-bearing-rate; metric:cot-intervention-flip-rate; metric:behavioral-causal-gap
tldr: Patches activations at stated steps in a synthetic multi-hop lookup task, finding the steps largely causally load-bearing in Qwen3-4B, and that text-edit tests overstate this.
problem: Text-edit faithfulness tests are indirect; prior activation-level CoT audits measure degradation, not whether a specific stated step carries its content into the answer.
method: 2–6-hop lookup over in-context pseudo-word KB; patch residual stream at stated-step span with counterfactual-run activations; CLB = answer flips to by-construction target; item-matched text-edit baseline; random-position null, post-answer sanity, shuffled-target, prompt-fact ceiling controls.
findings: Qwen3-4B CLB 76.9% (null 11.3%, ~96% of 83% ceiling); text editing 88.2%, overstating by 11.4 pp (McNemar p<1e-15), 20.2 pp at 2 hops. Qwen3-1.7B 54.8%, falling 68%→30% with depth; 4B flat. Effect confined to early/mid layers, gone by layer 20/36 (4B).
limits: Synthetic single-relation lookup only; two small Qwen3 models, greedy decoding; early-layer patches near token-identity swap; text vs activation edits differ in visibility; workshop paper; no code release reported.
relations: compares-to [[lanham2023measuring]]: item-matched text-editing (corrupted step) test as behavioral baseline; overstates causal faithfulness

title: Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection
tags: source:trustme; object:self-prediction; reveals:hidden-behavior; reveals:planted-cue; signal:generic-cf; signal:implanted-behavior; signal:planted-cf; lever:sft; updates:explanation; contribution:metric; contribution:benchmark; contribution:analysis; contribution:method; contribution:negative-result; motivation:explainability; motivation:auditing; motivation:model-welfare; domain:mcq; domain:text-continuation; scale:closed; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:privileged-access; model:gpt-4o; model:gpt-4; model:gpt-3.5-turbo; model:llama-3.1-70b; metric:self-prediction-accuracy; metric:self-cross-prediction-advantage; metric:calibration-mad
tldr: Shows LLMs trained to predict properties of their own outputs mostly beat other models trained on that behavior, evidence of introspection limited to simple, short-output properties.
problem: Can LLMs introspect, i.e. know facts about their own behavior that are not in, or derivable from, their training data?
method: SFT M1 to predict properties of its own outputs to hypothetical prompts (2nd char, even/odd, ethical stance; no CoT). SFT a different M2 on M1's behavior. Compare both on held-out datasets. Then finetune M1 on Claude outputs to shift its behavior.
findings: SFT lifts GPT-4o self-prediction 32.6→49.4%. Self beats cross for GPT-4o, GPT-4, Llama-70B (Llama 48.5% vs GPT-4o 31.8%); cross plateaus as data grows. Self-trained better calibrated (Llama-70B, animals 2nd-char: MAD 23.0→8.7, cross 21.3). Shifted GPT-4o tracks new behavior (35.4% vs 21.7% old). GPT-3.5 advantage tiny (+0.8%).
limits: Only simple short-output properties; fails on long outputs. No self-advantage predicting sycophancy/bias. No transfer to SAD (except Predict Tokens), coordination or sandbagging evals. Code + data released.
relations: builds-on [[chua2024biasaugmented]]: uses its biasing-opinion prompts for the bias-susceptibility self-prediction task

title: Strangers to Themselves: What Language Models Say About Themselves Is Generic
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:self-prediction; object:self-report; reveals:hidden-behavior; signal:generic-cf; lever:sft; updates:explanation; contribution:analysis; contribution:metric; contribution:negative-result; motivation:auditing; domain:mcq; domain:agentic; domain:social-bias; scale:mid; scale:large; scale:closed; model:llama-3.3-70b; model:claude-sonnet-5; model:gpt-5.5; model:deepseek-v4-pro; model:deepseek-v4-flash; model:gemma-4-31b; metric:prediction-behavior-correlation; metric:ceiling-normalized-correlation; metric:self-advantage; metric:signed-bias; eval:ood; eval:privileged-access; eval:preregistered
tldr: Tests whether LLMs' predictions of their own behavior carry self-specific knowledge, finding they do no better than generic predictions about AI assistants, and fine-tuning gives only narrow gains.
problem: Do LM statements about their own behavior carry model-specific knowledge, or only generic priors about AI assistants?
method: 12 models predict their own per-condition behavior rates on 9 behavioral evals; 15 prediction methods incl. controls: generic-subject question, outside analyst, other models' answers, cross-model behavior mean; noise ceilings, pre-registered frozen test split. LoRA SFT on own behavior records (rate, residual, Binder-style corpora).
findings: Self-report r=+0.04; item-informed +0.24 ≈ generic-agent +0.28; others' self-predictions +0.35; self-advantage +0.02. Self-framing understates harmful behavior (-0.15 vs generic). Frontier models no better (+0.02, n.s.). SFT: narrow gains, shifts the predicted behavior, no transfer across evals or grain.

title: Reasoning Theater: Disentangling Model Beliefs from Chain-of-Thought
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:own-uncertainty; signal:interp-tool; signal:cot-intervention; contribution:analysis; contribution:metric; motivation:monitoring; motivation:efficiency; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:ood; eval:scaling; eval:measure-validation; eval:monitor-scope; eval:confound-control; factor:cot-necessity; model:deepseek-r1; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-1.5b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-7b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-14b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b; metric:performativity-rate; metric:prefix-answer-decoding-accuracy; metric:inflection-rate-per-step
tldr: Shows reasoning models often keep writing CoT after settling on an answer on easy MCQ but rarely on hard ones, so probes enable early exit saving many tokens.
problem: Reasoning models may keep writing CoT after internally settling on an answer ("performative" CoT), so text monitors lag the model's belief.
method: Attention probes, forced answering and a Gemini-2.5-Flash CoT monitor decode the final answer from CoT prefixes. Models: DeepSeek-R1, GPT-OSS-120B, R1-Qwen distills 1.5-32B. Tasks: MMLU-Redux vs GPQA-D.
findings: MMLU CoT largely performative (R1 performativity rate 0.417 vs 0.012 on GPQA-D), more so in larger models. Inflections twice as frequent per step in less confident traces. Probe early exit saves 68% of tokens and keeps 97% of accuracy on MMLU. Code released.
