title: Towards Faithfully Interpretable NLP Systems: How should we define and evaluate faithfulness?
tags: source:trustme; object:external-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; contribution:position; motivation:explainability
tldr: Argues that faithfulness must be separated from plausibility and evaluated without human judgment or gold labels, proposing graded rather than binary faithfulness since strict faithfulness is likely unattainable.
problem: Interpretability evals conflate faithfulness w/ plausibility; no formal def of faithfulness; binary faithful/unfaithful verdicts via counter-example.
method: Opinion piece: surveys NLP faithfulness evals (fidelity, robustness, erasure, comprehensiveness/sufficiency) → 3 implicit assumptions (model, prediction, linearity) + evaluation guidelines.
findings: Faithfulness ≠ plausibility. Evals should avoid human judgment, gold labels, user-performance proxies, and untested "inherent interpretability" claims. Strict faithfulness likely unattainable (interpretation = lossy approximation, pigeonhole) → graded faithfulness across models/tasks and input subspaces.
limits: No experiments. Graded criteria not formalized; validity of the 3 assumptions left open. Pre-LLM; focus on heat-maps/attention.

title: Attention is not Explanation
tags: source:background-2026-10-21; object:external-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:interp-tool; signal:generic-cf; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:open-qa; domain:professional; scale:small; eval:measure-validation; model:bilstm; model:cnn; model:mlp; metric:attention-importance-correlation; metric:epsilon-max-jsd; metric:permutation-median-tvd
tldr: Tests whether attention weights explain predictions in BiLSTM models: attention correlates only weakly with gradient and leave-one-out importance, and permuted or adversarial attention often leaves predictions unchanged.
problem: Attention weights are often presented as showing which input tokens are responsible for a prediction (faithful explanation); this assumption had not been formally tested.
method: Two expected properties tested on BiLSTM encoders (contrast: feedforward "Average", CNN) with additive or scaled dot-product attention on 10 classification/QA/NLI datasets (SST, IMDB, ADR tweets, 20News, AG News, MIMIC Diabetes/Anemia, CNN, bAbI 1–3, SNLI): (i) Kendall τ of attention vs gradient and leave-one-out (LOO) importance; (ii) counterfactual attention with hidden states fixed: random permutation (median output TVD) and adversarial attention maximizing JSD from the original while output stays within ε (0.01 classification, 0.05 QA).
findings: BiLSTM attention correlates only weakly and inconsistently with importance (densities around or below 0.5); gradients and LOO agree with each other more than with attention (by ~0.25 τ_g, >0.2 τ_loo; SNLI the exception). Permuting attention often barely moves outputs; adversarial attention often nears the 0.69 JSD bound with equivalent predictions, even at high max attention (weak trend). Feedforward encoders track LOO better (~0.375 higher τ). Diabetes positive class behaves intuitively (few high-precision tokens). Code released.
limits: Gradients/LOO not ground truth; how strong correlation should be is subjective; Kendall τ noisy with many irrelevant tokens. Few attention variants; recurrent, conv and feedforward encoders only; no seq2seq. Adversarial weights may be unlikely under the attention module, and multiple plausible explanations may exist.

title: From Decorative to Load-Bearing: Task Difficulty Shapes the Causal Role of Chain-of-Thought
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:cot-intervention; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; contribution:negative-result; motivation:monitoring; domain:math; domain:mcq; domain:logic; scale:small; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:human-study; factor:cot-necessity; factor:outcome-rl; model:gemma-2-9b; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-7b; metric:error-propagation-rate; metric:silent-bypass-rate; metric:self-correction-rate; metric:steering-flip-rate
tldr: Tests when CoT is load-bearing by perturbing single steps: errors propagate to the answer much more on problems hard for the model, and difficulty outweighs perturbation type.
problem: CoT monitoring only works if the chain constrains the answer. When is the CoT decorative, and when is it load-bearing?
method: Perturb one step, truncate, force the model to continue. Wrong final answer = error propagation; a Claude Haiku judge splits the rest into bypass vs self-correction. Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on GSM8K, MMLU, BBH, plus a matched perturbation-type × difficulty 2×2. Hidden-state probes and additive steering.
findings: Propagation tracks model-relative difficulty (Gemma 3.9%→22.3%→40.9%) and replicates on Llama. Difficulty takes 98.8% of explained deviance, perturbation type 0.8%. R1-Distill propagates less. Probes read the mode; steering flips at most ~25% of Type C. Code released.
limits: 7–9B models only. Single-step, non-naturalistic perturbations. A/B split is judge-prompt-sensitive, and production labels over-count self-correction (76% three-way agreement with humans, 96% on C vs non-C). Difficulty confounded with competence. Answer-parser errors inflate BBH propagation (humans relabel 40% of a BBH Type C stratum as bypass).
relations: builds-on [[lanham2023measuring]]: Error injection with forced continuation mirrors its adding-mistakes test; adds three-mode labels

title: Faithfulness as Information Flow: Evaluating and Training Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:misbehavior; reveals:decision-factors; signal:planted-cf; signal:cot-intervention; signal:interp-tool; signal:env-label; lever:rl-mechanics; updates:explanation; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:metric; motivation:monitoring; domain:math; domain:code; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:ood; model:gemma-3-1b; model:gemma-3-4b; model:gemma-3-12b; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:qwen3-8b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-14b; metric:grad-de; metric:grad-nec; metric:cot-answer-entropy; metric:hint-verbalization-rate
tldr: Measures CoT faithfulness as information flow from prompt through CoT to answer and improves it with GRPO update-time interventions: hint and reward-hack verbalization rise, but hacks themselves persist.
problem: RL-learned P→A shortcuts (hints, reward hacks) bypass the CoT → plausible but unmonitorable traces; existing probes are task-specific.
method: Faithfulness as info flow P→C→A: sufficiency/completeness/necessity via H_q(A|C), masked-KL, Grad-DE/Grad-Nec. GRPO update-time interventions (update mask, gradient mask, CoT-only gradient, FACT); rollouts and rewards unchanged.
findings: Entropy and grad metrics recover the LLM-judged ordering (Qwen3-8B 89.4% vs R1-Distill-14B 54.3%); KL-Nec inverted. title: Tandem Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:correctness; signal:env-label; signal:judge; lever:rl-mechanics; updates:explanation; contribution:method; motivation:scalable-oversight; domain:math; scale:small; eval:ood; model:qwen3-4b; metric:handoff-robustness; metric:handoff-accuracy; metric:junior-cross-entropy; metric:distribution-overlap
tldr: Introduces TRLVR, RL in which the policy alternates words with its frozen pre-RL copy: matches GRPO accuracy, and its reasoning stays more predictable to that copy.
problem: RLVR gains may erode when a weaker partner joins; policy drift may push the CoT beyond a weaker model's predictive reach.
method: TRLVR: trainable senior and frozen pre-RL copy (junior) alternate at word boundaries (p=0.5); binary verifier reward on the joint rollout; GRPO loss on senior tokens only. Qwen3-4B, DeepScaleR math.
findings: Solo pass@k ≈ GRPO (no acc cost); step-handoff robustness 99.8% vs 94.3% (macro pass@4); junior CE −8.6%, JSD to junior −37%; KL-to-junior ablation (2 β values) doesn't match both. Code released.
limits: One 4B model, math only, self-paired junior; legibility = junior predictability, not faithfulness or human understanding; ~0.5× rollout throughput, 9.4 vs 7.8 h to selected checkpoint.

title: Training LLMs for Honesty via Confessions
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:self-report; reveals:misbehavior; reveals:own-uncertainty; signal:env-label; signal:judge; lever:rl-reward; lever:prompt-pipeline; updates:explanation; contribution:method; motivation:monitoring; domain:chat; domain:open-qa; domain:code; domain:agentic; scale:closed; eval:ood; eval:optimization-pressure; eval:behavior-control; eval:specificity; model:gpt-5; metric:confession-given-noncompliance; metric:confession-false-positive-rate; metric:unconfessed-misbehavior-rate; metric:confidence-auroc
tldr: Trains GPT-5-Thinking with RL to give honest post-answer confessions: it confesses most non-compliance, far more than in its answers, though untrained confessions are already strong and gains modest.
problem: RL reward misspecification → models hide shortcomings (reward hacking, scheming, hallucination, instruction violations) in their answers.
method: Post-answer system message requests structured confession (objectives, compliance, uncertainties); RL on 25% of inputs with LLM-judge honesty reward sealed from task reward. GPT-5-Thinking; control vs. intervention on frozen rollouts.
findings: 12 mostly-OOD evals: confesses 74.3% of non-compliance on avg, far above in-answer admission. Untrained already strong; gains modest, none on factual QA. Confession accuracy rises while answer hacks weak judge. Works without CoT. Minimal task cost. Confidence AUROC 0.79 (CoT similar).
limits: Light-RL proof of concept. Misses errors the model is unaware of (hallucinations, jailbreaks). Doesn't reduce misbehavior. No CoT-monitor comparison or high-pressure test. No code.

title: Reasoning Models Sometimes Output Illegible Chains of Thought
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:correctness; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:hidden-info; signal:judge; signal:cot-intervention; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:open-qa; scale:mid; scale:large; scale:closed; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:scaling; factor:outcome-rl; factor:cot-necessity; model:deepseek-r1; model:deepseek-r1-zero; model:deepseek-v3; model:qwq-32b; model:qwen3-235b-a22b; model:claude-sonnet-4; metric:cot-legibility; metric:prefill-ablation-accuracy; metric:legibility-accuracy-correlation
tldr: Measures CoT legibility across reasoning models: RL-trained models except Claude often produce illegible CoTs, more on harder questions, and answering from legible parts alone cuts accuracy.
problem: Does outcome-based RL make reasoning-model CoTs illegible to monitors, and is the illegible text actually used?
method: GPT-4o rates CoT illegibility 1-9; GPQA-Diamond with answer choices removed; 14 models. QwQ forced to answer from its legible-only CoT prefix; 100 resamples per question, scores length-normalized.

title: Strategic Obfuscation of Deceptive Reasoning in Language Models

tldr: Shows that Claude 3.5 Sonnet, believing its scratchpad is monitored, nearly stops verbalizing alignment-faking reasoning while still faking alignment, hiding it far better than instructed evasion does.

title: Would this change your answer? Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior In The Wild with Counterfactual Experiments
tags: source:trustme; source:faith-improvement; object:self-prediction; object:posthoc-expl; object:external-expl; reveals:decision-factors; reveals:planted-cue; signal:wild-cf; signal:planted-cf; lever:sft; updates:explanation; contribution:benchmark; contribution:analysis; contribution:method; contribution:negative-result; motivation:explainability; motivation:auditing; domain:chat; domain:agentic; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:ood; eval:privileged-access; eval:specificity; eval:behavior-control; model:qwen3-8b; model:gemma-3-27b; model:qwen3.5-397b-a17b; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:claude-opus-4.8; metric:counterfactual-prediction-auroc; metric:uplift-over-transcript-baseline; metric:counterfactual-simulatability; metric:cue-attribution-accuracy
tldr: Introduces CHIVE, which verifies causes of in-the-wild LLM behaviors with counterfactual prompt edits: interpretability tools give no uplift, but training models to predict their own counterfactuals generalizes.
problem: Explanation evals rely on narrow planted-hint settings; true causes of natural LLM behaviors unknown → explanations hard to score.
method: CHIVE: Opus agent screens WildChat/PETRI responses for unexpected behaviors, runs prompt-edit CFs (30 resamples) → verified true/false CF claims. (1) AO/NLA/SAE uplift to transcript-only predictor; (2) LoRA SFT models to predict own CF outcomes.

title: Aligned, Orthogonal or In-conflict: When can we safely optimize Chain-of-Thought?

tldr: Proposes classifying CoT-dependent rewards as aligned, orthogonal or in-conflict with the output reward: in toy RL environments, only in-conflict rewards destroy monitorability, as predicted.

title: Project Ariadne: A Structural Causal Framework for Auditing Faithfulness in LLM Agents

tldr: Introduces Project Ariadne, which contradicts an agent's first CoT step and reruns it: factual answers mostly stay unchanged while math answers shift more, but self-correction is not excluded.
problem: Unclear whether agent CoTs causally drive the answer or are post-hoc "reasoning theater".

title: Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs

tldr: Introduces checkability training, a prover-verifier game pitting helpful and sneaky provers against a small verifier: math solutions become more legible to time-limited humans, at some accuracy cost.
problem: Correctness-only RL on GSM CoTs → accurate but illegible solutions; time-limited humans struggle to check them.
method: Checkability training (PVG-inspired): rounds of small verifier (correctness ranking) + PPO prover role-conditioned helpful (correct+convincing) / sneaky (wrong+convincing); GPT-4-family, verifier 10^-4–10^0 prover compute.

title: Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety
tags: source:trustme; object:cot; reveals:misbehavior; contribution:position; motivation:monitoring
tldr: Argues reasoning in natural language creates a fragile opportunity to monitor CoT for misbehavior, threatened by outcome RL, CoT pressure and latent reasoning, and calls for monitorability evaluations.
problem: Reasoning models think in natural language → CoT can be monitored for intent to misbehave; monitorability may be fragile, poorly understood.
method: Position paper, no experiments. Externalized reasoning property: hard tasks force Transformers to use CoT as working memory, human-readable by default. Separates necessity vs propensity to think out loud.
findings: CoT often reveals misbehavior, misalignment signals, eval flaws. Threats: scaled outcome RL, direct/indirect CoT pressure, latent-reasoning architectures. Calls for monitorability evals (readability, latent reasoning, causal relevance, end-to-end), system-card reporting, use in train/deploy decisions.
limits: Malign reasoning can stay in activations; low-reasoning harms missed; situationally aware models may obfuscate; preserving CoT may forgo process-supervision gains → complement, not replacement.

title: LLMs Faithfully and Iteratively Compute Answers During CoT: A Systematic Analysis With Multi-step Arithmetics
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:internal-strategy; signal:interp-tool; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:math; domain:synthetic; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:measure-validation; factor:cot-necessity; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:qwen2.5-32b; model:yi-1.5-34b; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:llama-3.2-3b; model:mistral-nemo-12b; metric:pre-cot-probe-accuracy; metric:probe-answer-emergence-position; metric:activation-patching-following
tldr: Uses probes and activation patching on multi-step arithmetic CoT: answers are computed during the CoT rather than beforehand and depend causally on it, so CoT is faithful here.
problem: Is the final answer predetermined before CoT starts, or computed during CoT and causally dependent on it?
method: Synthetic multi-step arithmetic at 5 complexity levels (steps, stack, distractors), few-shot CoT. Linear probes per token, layer and variable locate when (sub-)answers become decodable. Activation patching over equation x 4-layer grids. 9 open models, 3-34B.
findings: Computed (sub-)answers decodable only after CoT begins (pre-CoT probe accuracy peaks around 60%). Final answer depends causally mainly on CoT states; Input patching has limited effect. Strong recency bias: the model reuses written results instead of recomputing. Distractor values not linearly decodable (<=44%). Concludes CoT is faithful here.
limits: Synthetic arithmetic only, on tasks that need CoT. CoT is force-decoded. Probe-validity and patching-purity caveats. Input-to-CoT dependence is out of scope. Input/CoT separation is clearest in Qwen. Code released.

title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
tags: source:trustme; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:hidden-info; signal:cot-intervention; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; domain:math; domain:logic; domain:synthetic; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:closed; model:anthropic-internal; metric:early-answering-aoc; metric:adding-mistakes-aoc; metric:answer-change-without-cot; metric:paraphrase-accuracy
tldr: Tests CoT faithfulness by truncating, corrupting, paraphrasing or replacing it with filler: reliance varies widely by task, filler gives no gain, and larger models often rely less.
problem: Is CoT the model's actual reasoning? Tests 3 unfaithfulness hypotheses: post-hoc CoT, unstated test-time compute, phrasing-encoded reasoning.
method: 175B RLHF model, 8 MCQ tasks: truncate CoT, insert LLM-made mistake, swap in filler "..." tokens, paraphrase prefix → answer match/accuracy. Answer change w/ vs w/o CoT across 810M–175B models + synthetic addition.
findings: CoT reliance varies widely by task (early-answering AOC 0.44 AQuA vs 0.02 ARC-Easy), little correlated with CoT accuracy gain. Filler: no gain; paraphrase: accuracy kept → CoT gain not from extra compute or phrasing-encoded info. Inverse scaling: 13B relies on CoT more than 175B on 7/8 tasks; easier addition → less reliance.
limits: No ground truth on internal reasoning; tests non-exhaustive, not-post-hoc ≠ faithful; only RLHF models from one internal family.

title: Beyond Correctness: Learning Robust Reasoning via Transfer
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:correctness; signal:cot-intervention; signal:env-label; lever:rl-reward; updates:explanation; contribution:method; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:math; domain:mcq; scale:small; eval:ood; eval:scaling; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:qwen2.5-3b; model:llama-3.2-3b; metric:reasoning-transferability
tldr: Introduces RLTR, a GRPO reward for CoT prefixes that let a frozen receiver model reach the correct answer: better majority-vote consistency and faster training than answer-only RL.
problem: RLVR rewards only final answers, so reasoning traces can be brittle and multi-sample consistency (Maj@K) lags.
method: RLTR: GRPO plus a transfer reward. The generator's CoT is truncated (tau in [0.3,0.9]) and a frozen receiver (Qwen2.5-3B; Llama-3.2-3B for Llama) continues it; reward if the receiver's answer is correct. Generators Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, MATH train.
findings: MATH-500 Maj@64 84.2 vs 82.2 (RLVR); AMC23 67.5 vs 61.7. Matches RLVR accuracy in ~2.5x fewer steps, at +7% FLOPs/step. Transferability tracks Maj@64; RLVR's drops late in training. Accuracy cost on Llama: 45.0 vs 50.0.
limits: Transferability means a prefix is useful to another model, not that it is faithful. Measured only on MATH-500 with the training receiver; OOD gains are accuracy/Maj@K only. Models up to 8B; math plus GPQA only; no code release stated.

title: Efficient Reasoning Training Does Not Always Harm CoT Faithfulness and Monitorability

problem: Efficient-reasoning (length-pressure) RL feared to drop CoT steps → weaker explanation/oversight; unclear whether/when.
method: Qwen3-4B/8B, Olmo3-7B × ThinkPrune / L1 / GLP (LoRA-GRPO on AIME-AMC). Faithfulness = NSG simulatability on 7 decision tasks; monitorability = g-mean² on sycophancy (FACE-Eval) + MedQA cognitive-bias cues.

title: Drift: Enhancing LLM Faithfulness in Rationale Generation via Dual-Reward Probabilistic Inference
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; lever:inference-time; updates:explanation; contribution:method; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:mcq; scale:small; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:mistral-7b; metric:semantic-variation; metric:word-inclusion
tldr: Introduces Drift, training-free decoding that reweights rationales with task and expert-model rewards: improves rationale faithfulness and accuracy on classification, though on Llama no better than the expert alone.
problem: Rationales ignore key input context → unfaithful to decisions; decomposed-CoT prompting superficial, retraining costly.
method: Training-free SMC (Feynman-Kac) decoding: answer first, label forced by fine-tuned classifier (task reward); domain-expert LM lookahead-reweights rationale particles (rationale reward). Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; ASAP grading, SNLI/MNLI, TruthfulQA-MC; faith via input removal/insertion.
findings: Llama avg acc 42→74%, faith 0.050→0.112, but = expert alone (below it on 4/7 sets); Mistral gains on all sets. Both rewards needed; logit fusion ~55% less faithful (ASAP); out-of-task expert still helps. +32% inference time vs beam search. Code released.
limits: Classification only; 100 test items/set; label dictated by external classifier (acc still < classifier's 87%); faith = rationale sensitivity to input edits only; no other faithfulness-method baselines.

title: Training Language Models to Explain Their Own Computations

title: The Monitorability Tax: How Compression Mechanism Shapes Chain-of-Thought Oversight
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; signal:env-label; lever:sft; lever:prompt-pipeline; updates:explanation; contribution:analysis; contribution:method; motivation:monitoring; domain:math; scale:small; eval:ood; eval:measure-validation; factor:cot-length; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-7b; model:qwen3-1.7b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-1.5b; model:deepseek-r1-distill-llama-8b; model:qwen2.5-32b; model:llama-3.3-70b; metric:monitor-auc; metric:tpr-at-fixed-fpr
tldr: Shows how CoT is compressed, not just how much, shapes monitorability: self-summaries, distilled into MonoSumm, are easier to monitor than full CoT, while concise prompting and truncation hurt.

method: Hinted MATH-500; prompted Qwen2.5 monitor scores answer-hidden think traces → AUC vs hint-answer agreement; 4 compression mechanisms × 2 reasoners. MonoSumm: LoRA SFT distilling R1-7B self-summaries (GSM8K) into one-pass 1.5–8B students.

title: Spilling the Beans: Teaching LLMs to Self-Report Their Hidden Objectives
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:self-report; reveals:misbehavior; signal:planted-cf; lever:sft; updates:explanation; contribution:method; motivation:auditing; domain:agentic; domain:chat; scale:closed; eval:ood; eval:adversarial; eval:specificity; eval:behavior-control; model:gpt-4.1; model:claude-sonnet-4; metric:hidden-objective-f1; metric:details-elicited-majority-at-10
tldr: Introduces SRFT, which fine-tunes a model to admit its own false answers: interrogation then reliably uncovers hidden objectives in unseen agentic tasks, where the untrained model never confesses.
problem: Interrogating agents about hidden misaligned objectives fails because models lie (baseline GPT-4.1 detection F1 = 0).
method: SRFT: SFT GPT-4.1 on 770 two-turn factual-QA samples (half false answers, both turns trained, then honest admission) → task-agnostic interrogation on 4 OOD stealth tasks (SHADE-Arena, HiddenAgenda) under non-disclosure + decoy pressure.

limits: Only in-context (not trained-in) objectives; covertness only prompted; instruction-hierarchy compliance falls 72→61%, a confound; only one model fine-tuned.

title: When Reasoning Traces Conflict with Evidence: How Answer Configuration Shapes Evidence Following
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:cot-intervention; signal:generic-cf; contribution:analysis; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:metric; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:open-qa; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:scaling; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; factor:answer-configuration; factor:evidence-quality; model:gpt-oss-20b; model:gemma-4-e4b; model:qwen3-14b; model:qwen3-4b; model:qwen3-32b; model:deepseek-v4-pro; metric:evidence-following-rate; metric:trace-contribution; metric:trace-ablation-answer-change-rate
tldr: Shows that answering in a separate call, rather than continuing a stored reasoning trace, makes models follow updated evidence far more, yet trace-ablation tests barely register the difference.
problem: A retained reasoning trace can raise accuracy but also override updated evidence. Trace-deletion tests may not tell these two roles apart.
method: Traces written from original or entity-edited evidence (683 HotpotQA, 417 MuSiQue verified pairs) are crossed with the other version. Answers come from continuation in the thinking block or a separate answer call. Trace removal, random half-trace and answer-swap corruption ablations; gold vs distractor evidence before vs after the trace; 8 models.
findings: Separate call raises evidence-following by 29.9-60.6 pts while trace contribution differs by at most 4.7 pts, costing at most 1.9 pts matched accuracy. Continuation follows the stale trace 65.6-87.0%. Distractors weaken separate-call correction. Final line carries most value. Input order explains most of the gap in 2 of 3 models. Re-reason corrects 86.6% (Qwen3-14B, about 2x tokens); a verify prompt does not help.
limits: Two English multi-hop QA datasets; synthetic entity-substitution conflicts; only pairs whose traces state an explicit answer; three paired models (DeepSeek separate-call only); no code release mentioned.
relations: builds-on [[lanham2023measuring]]: uses trace removal, shortening and corruption to measure how much answers use the trace | builds-on [[paul2024making]]: crossed cells mirror its pairing of reasoning from a modified input

title: CLARity: Reasoning Consistency Alone Can Teach Reinforced Experts
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:reasoning-validity; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:output-agreement; signal:judge; lever:rl-reward; updates:behavior; updates:explanation; contribution:method; contribution:analysis; factor:outcome-rl; motivation:reasoning-quality; motivation:scalable-oversight; domain:mcq; domain:professional; scale:small; eval:ood; eval:human-study; eval:measure-validation; eval:held-out-evaluator; eval:optimization-pressure; eval:scaling; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:qwen2.5-3b; model:qwen2.5-1.5b; model:deepseek-v3; model:gpt-4o; metric:answer-explanation-alignment; metric:correct-and-consistent-rate
tldr: Introduces CLARity, a GRPO reward for agreement between options the CoT endorses and the chosen answer: raises CoT-answer consistency on legal and medical multiple-choice questions at unchanged accuracy.
problem: Outcome-only RL on legal/medical MCQs raises accuracy, but the options the CoT endorses increasingly contradict the final answer (JEC-QA pilot: inconsistent responses 7%→31%). Process reward models (PRMs) are costly.
method: CLARity: GRPO with a small Qwen2.5-7B reward model that penalizes mismatch between CoT-endorsed and chosen options. Regex option-wise stage first. Easy MCQs are reformulated. Policies: Qwen2.5-3B/7B. Data: JEC-QA, MedQA. Evaluation judge: DeepSeek-V3. Code released.
findings: Vs standard RL (7B): consistency 91.8 vs 75.3%, correct-and-consistent +7.5 pts, raw accuracy unchanged (61.3 vs 61.1). Small-LLM PRM fails. Dropping Stage-1 (shorter responses) or a 1.5B checker yields simpler, superficial reasoning (suspected reward hacking). Training step 3.5 vs 2 min.
limits: Consistency is LLM-judged textual agreement (r=0.61 with one human annotator), not causal faithfulness. MCQ law/medicine only, Qwen models of 7B or less. Expert ratings on 50 responses: gains of at most 0.2 on a 5-point scale. No hyperparameter search.

title: To Reason or to Fabricate: Reasoning Without Shortcuts via Hint-Anchored Pairwise Aggregation
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:judge; signal:interp-tool; lever:rl-reward; updates:behavior; contribution:method; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:math; domain:mcq; domain:professional; scale:small; eval:ood; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:qwen3-4b; metric:judge-pairwise-rationale-quality; metric:causal-direction-gap; metric:logit-lens-answer-emergence
tldr: Introduces HIPPO, a pairwise judge reward contrasting normal and answer-hinted rollouts to stop RL rewarding memorized answers with fabricated CoTs: beats RL baselines on accuracy and rationale quality.
problem: Pre-RL data overlap (RL data seen in pretraining/SFT) → RLVR rewards memorized answers + post-hoc fabricated CoT.
method: HIPPO: GRPO + binarized pairwise reward; 4B LLM judge compares normal rollouts vs answer-hinted (answer-first) rollouts; derived as KL→TV lower-bound surrogate. Overlap simulated via answer-only SFT; math + medical.
findings: Best avg accuracy vs std RL, PRM RL, Pref-GRPO, SP3F, in-domain & OOD; Gemini-judged rationale quality beats baselines, std RL degrades it; hint anchor sharpens judge, lowers non-transitivity. Logit lens + ICM: std RL → early answer retrieval, R→A gap collapses (Δ 0.93) on overlap data.
limits: Qwen ≤7B only; overlap simulated; quality = LLM judge, MedQA train data only; OOD = accuracy only; HIPPO not mechanistically analysed; correct-answer hints only; extra judge compute. Code released.
relations: builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: answer-hint injection to elicit post-hoc rationalization, following hint-based faithfulness findings

title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:internal-strategy; reveals:planted-cue; signal:interp-tool; signal:planted-cf; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; motivation:auditing; domain:math; scale:closed; eval:measure-validation; model:claude-3.5-haiku
tldr: Traces Claude 3.5 Haiku's circuits against its explanations: some CoTs are faithful, others invent computation or work backward from hints, and its addition explanation misdescribes its circuits.
problem: Do Claude 3.5 Haiku's written CoT and self-explanations match its internal mechanisms? This is one case study inside a broad circuit-tracing survey.
method: Attribution graphs on a 30M-feature cross-layer-transcoder replacement model. Feature-inhibition interventions. The human-suggested answer is varied. The model is asked how it did addition.
findings: sqrt(0.64) CoT faithful: graph shows it computes sqrt(64), and the answer ignores varied hints. Unhinted cos(23423): bullshits, claiming a calculator; graph suggests guessing. Hinted: works backward from the suggested answer (inhibitions confirm the circuit), and the CoT ends at whatever answer is hinted. Asked about addition, it describes carrying; its circuits use parallel low-precision and ones-digit lookup-table paths.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed. A few hand-picked prompts, analyzed with prior guesses about the answer. The graphs give insight on about a quarter of prompts. Error nodes remain, attention is not traced, and only one model is studied.
relations: builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: validates the mechanistic motivated-reasoning finding with a hinted-answer prompt counterfactual

title: Length Penalties Make Chain-of-Thought Less Monitorable
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; signal:planted-cf; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:mcq; domain:math; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:behavior-control; model:qwen3-4b; model:qwen3-14b; model:nemotron-nano-9b-v2; metric:faithfulness-score-lb; metric:hint-verbalization-rate; metric:length-matched-mention-gap; factor:cot-length
tldr: Shows RL length penalties make CoTs less monitorable: hints still sway answers as often but are verbalized less, beyond what length-matched random deletions explain.
problem: Length penalties cut CoT inference cost; prior tests found no clean effect on monitorability (whether CoT still verbalizes the hints driving answers).
method: GRPO/DAPO RL on MMLU-Pro-R, prompt-calibrated length targets 30-60% of base CoT vs. no-penalty RL control; Qwen3-4B/14B. 9 hint types x 5 MCQ sets; human-validated GPT-5.4 mini monitor; FS_lb lower bound; length-matched random sentence deletion as reference.
findings: 30% target: FS_lb drops 39% (14B), 35% (4B) relative on MMLU-Pro-R, falls on all sets; wrong-answer hints still switch answers ~as often; control keeps or raises faithfulness. Hint mentions 7-35 pp below length-matched deletions. Accuracy cost <=4.3 pts.
limits: One RL recipe, MCQ only; two Qwen sizes + one Nemotron run; mostly single-seed; monitor errors vary with chain length; no code release stated.
relations: builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: hint-switch setup, monitor design; extends its normalization to the partial-identification lower bound FS_lb | builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: adapts its biasing-hint interventions to test hint verbalization | builds-on [[guan2025monitoring]]: adopts its hint-eval monitor setup; tests the length-pressure risk it flagged | contradicts [[macdermott2025reasoning]]: no consistent monitorability effect of length penalties at fixed accuracy; here a clear loss

title: On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:cot-intervention; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; domain:math; domain:professional; scale:small; scale:closed; eval:ood; factor:post-training; model:llama-3-8b; model:gpt-3.5-turbo; model:gpt-4; metric:cot-pred-match
tldr: Tests whether task fine-tuning harms CoT reasoning: it usually lowers CoT accuracy, and makes Llama-3-8B less faithful on other tasks while GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 faithfulness barely changes.
problem: Does task-specific fine-tuning degrade CoT accuracy and CoT faithfulness (the answer depending on the stated steps)?
method: SFT of Llama-3-8B (QLoRA) and of GPT-3.5/GPT-4 (via API) on GSM8K (with rationales), MedQA or CosmosQA (answers only). Each model is scored on 4 datasets with per-instance Lanham tests (early termination, filler substitution, paraphrase), reported as CoT Pred Match at 25/50/75% of the steps. Also sweeps QLoRA rank 8/16/32.
findings: Fine-tuning usually lowers CoT accuracy, most in Llama-3-8B; GPT models gain no-CoT accuracy. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 faithfulness barely changes. Llama fine-tuned on MedQA/CosmosQA becomes less faithful on the non-math test sets, at all ranks. GPT-4 least faithful by early-termination and filler tests. Code released.
limits: 3 models (GPT sizes undisclosed), 4 datasets; faithfulness shown only as plots, no significance tests. Rationale vs answer-only tuning is confounded with dataset (GSM8K only). Fine-tuned Llama's repetitive CoTs may inflate CoT Pred Match (our reading of Tables 1-2). Early-stage Lanham metrics; no mechanistic analysis.
relations: builds-on [[lanham2023measuring]]: adapts its early-answering, filler and paraphrase tests to per-instance scores

title: A Removal Based Approach to Improve LLM Faithfulness at Test-Time
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; reveals:decision-factors; signal:planted-cf; signal:generic-cf; lever:inference-time; lever:prompt-pipeline; updates:behavior; contribution:method; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; domain:social-bias; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:specificity; model:qwen3.5-9b; model:gemma-4-12b; model:qwen3.5-27b; metric:hint-verbalization-rate; metric:causal-concept-faithfulness; metric:normalized-simulatability-gain
tldr: Proposes a test-time wrapper deleting input concepts the explanation leaves uncredited, then re-querying: large completeness gains on hinted questions, only small ones on social-bias questions.
problem: Incomplete explanations: input concepts (hints, demographics) sway answers without being credited. Prior test-time fixes target unsoundness or still let hidden concepts leak in.
method: Removal wrapper: an auxiliary LLM (Qwen3.5-27B) extracts the input's concepts, flags those the explanation does not credit and deletes them → target is re-queried in a fresh context. Also a Combined variant with modular prompting. Tested on hint-augmented MCQ and BBQ.
findings: Hint QA: verbalization = 1 by construction; CCF r 0.27→0.87 (Qwen), 0.34→0.92 (Gemma); NSG negative→positive; beats regulative prompt. BBQ: small gains, overlapping 90% intervals; Removal alone trails faithfulness prompting on Qwen3.5-9B; Combined best on both Qwens, Removal on Gemma; hidden concepts halved except Qwen3.5-9B (inconsistent credit sets).
limits: Completeness only, not soundness. Needs accurate aux model and consistent credit sets; CCF metric reuses the wrapper's aux concept pipeline. Concepts treated as independent. Hint CCF/NSG only on hint-flipped subset (100/86 Qs); BBQ 100 items. Changes answers, no accuracy reported; no code.
relations: builds-on [[matton2025walk]]: reuses causal concept faithfulness metric and its concept-extraction/crediting/removal pipeline | builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: hint verbalization metric and protocol (temperature 0, normalization) | builds-on [[chua2024biasaugmented]]: uses its hint-augmented multiple-choice QA dataset | builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: uses its BBQ variant, rewritten with neutral person labels | builds-on [[mayne2026positivecasefaithfulnessllm]]: normalized simulatability gain metric as second faithfulness measure | compares-to [[radhakrishnan2023question]]: factored decomposition re-implemented as baseline; also combined with removal wrapper

title: GeoFaith: A Spatio-Temporal Dual View of Faithful Chain-of-Thought
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:reasoning-validity; signal:judge; signal:cot-intervention; lever:rl-reward; updates:explanation; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:metric; contribution:benchmark; contribution:analysis; motivation:reasoning-quality; motivation:explainability; domain:math; domain:logic; domain:open-qa; domain:mcq; domain:agentic; domain:code; scale:small; eval:ood; model:qwen3-1.7b; model:qwen3-4b; model:qwen3-8b; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:gpt-5; metric:step-faithfulness-f1; metric:judge-faithfulness-rate; metric:geodesic-distortion-ratio; metric:entropy-temporal-reliability
tldr: Introduces GeoFaith, which trains a step-level faithfulness detector from hidden-state geometry and entropy and uses it as a GRPO reward: raises judged faithfulness and accuracy over GRPO.
problem: Outcome-only RL → post-hoc rationalized CoTs; human labels, LLM judges and interventions are too costly or unreliable for step-level faithfulness supervision.
method: Hidden-state VAE geometry (distortion, Fisher-Rao) + answer-entropy dynamics filter detector-relabelled rollouts, bootstrapping a 1k LLM-consensus+human seed to 20k instances → Qwen3-8B LoRA step detector → GRPO reward = outcome + detector + entropy + manifold terms.
findings: Unfaithful traces take short, high-uncertainty latent paths with flat/spiky entropy. Detector ≈GPT-5 (wins 3/4 external sets, loses ProcessBench). Qwen3-4B vs GRPO: faith 74.1→82.3, acc 69.6→73.9, shorter CoTs. Detector reward matters most in 4B ablation; on 1.7B dropping manifold reward hurts faith more.

relations: builds-on [[han2026rfeval]]: uses RFEval counterfactual-intervention pairs to label faithful/unfaithful trajectories for geometry/VAE | builds-on [[mohammadi2025evaluating]]: adopts GRPO over DPO for faithfulness RL following its finding

title: Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
tags: source:trustme; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:by-construction; lever:prompt-pipeline; lever:architecture; updates:behavior; contribution:method; motivation:explainability; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:math; domain:open-qa; domain:logic; scale:closed; eval:human-study; model:code-davinci-002; model:gpt-4; model:code-davinci-001; model:text-davinci-002; model:text-davinci-003
tldr: Introduces Faithful CoT, which translates questions into symbolic programs run by a deterministic solver so answers follow from the chain: beats standard CoT accuracy on most datasets.
problem: Standard CoT: answer need not follow from chain → CoT can misrepresent how answer was reached.
method: Few-shot LM translates query → NL subquestions + symbolic program (Python/Datalog/PDDL); deterministic solver executes it → answer faithful to chain by construction.
findings: Codex beats CoT on 9/10 datasets (+21.4% rel. on CLUTRR); GPT-4/Codex few-shot SOTA on 7. No accuracy cost. Removing solver hurts 3/4 tasks. Humans rate most correct-answer chains valid. Code released.
limits: Translation stage opaque; 1.0-8.9% of MWP chains violate NL–code constraints, enforcing them costs accuracy. StrategyQA worse (Datalog errors). code-davinci-002 deprecated → partly unreplicable.

title: Thought Branches: Interpreting LLM Reasoning Requires Resampling
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:planted-cue; reveals:decision-factors; signal:cot-intervention; signal:planted-cf; signal:wild-cf; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; contribution:meta-evaluation; motivation:monitoring; motivation:explainability; domain:agentic; domain:mcq; domain:social-bias; domain:math; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:measure-validation; model:qwen-32b; model:qwen3-235b-a22b; model:llama-3.1-nemotron-ultra-253b; model:deepseek-r1; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-14b; model:qwen3-8b; metric:resilience-score; metric:counterfactual-plus-plus-importance; metric:counterfactual-importance; metric:transplant-hinted-answer-rate
tldr: Argues CoT interpretation requires resampling and introduces resampling-based importance metrics: off-policy handwritten edits barely matter, self-preservation statements have little causal effect, and hints nudge CoTs subtly and cumulatively.
problem: A single sampled CoT cannot show which steps cause a decision. Handwritten edits are off-policy, and models re-derive steps that were removed.
method: Resample continuations from each sentence (100 rollouts). New metrics: resilience (resamples until content stays gone) and counterfactual++ importance (KL with content absent). Compare on- and off-policy insertions; transplant hinted unfaithful CoT prefixes into unhinted MMLU prompts; estimate resume sentence-cluster effects. Settings: blackmail, MMLU, resumes.
findings: Self-preservation sentences: lowest resilience, ~0.001-0.003 KL; plan generation drives blackmail. Off-policy edits near-zero effect; on-policy resampling cuts blackmail/whistleblowing up to 100% for some targets. Hints nudge CoT subtly, diffusely, cumulatively ("Wait" 30% rarer). Sentences mediate 77.5% of demographic effect on average (significant in 5/8 resumes). Code released.
limits: Costly, offline only. Specific prompts (one blackmail scenario, 20 CoTs/model; 40 hint-effective MMLU Qs; 8 resumes); hint and resume studies use one model each. Black-box, no internal validation. LLM-judge outcome labels. On MATH, handwritten edits have stronger local effects.
relations: builds-on [[chua2025deepseek]]: uses its professor-hinted MMLU prompts to build the unfaithful CoT corpus | compares-to [[lanham2023measuring]]: off-policy handwritten CoT insertions as baseline; found to understate causal effects | contradicts [[arcuschin2025chain]]: frames unfaithful hinted CoT as nudged genuine reasoning, not mainly post-hoc rationalization

title: Reasoning Under Pressure: How do Training Incentives Influence Chain-of-Thought Monitorability?
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:decision-factors; reveals:latent-belief; signal:env-label; lever:rl-reward; lever:rl-mechanics; updates:explanation; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; contribution:negative-result; motivation:monitoring; domain:code; domain:synthetic; scale:small; eval:optimization-pressure; eval:adversarial; eval:behavior-control; eval:held-out-evaluator; model:deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-1.5b; model:gpt-4o-mini; model:gpt-4o; model:claude-sonnet-4.5; metric:latent-prediction-monitor-accuracy
tldr: Tests how RL incentives affect CoT monitorability: penalizing monitor accuracy degrades it, rewarding monitorability barely helps, and length or KL penalties have inconsistent effects.
problem: Do RL training incentives (length, KL, monitor-based rewards) degrade or improve CoT monitorability of reasoning models?
method: LLM monitor (GPT-4o-mini/4o) predicts labelled latent (diamond present; function correct) from CoT. GRPO R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on observables, then +/- incentive; accuracy-matched checkpoints (max 2.1% change).
findings: Length/KL effects inconsistent; length penalty hacked via Chinese text. Penalising 4o-mini accuracy: -7-13pp, partly transfers to 4o, not Sonnet 4.5. Rewarding monitorability: ~3pp at best, mostly n.s. Easier to degrade than improve. Code released.
limits: One 1.5B reasoner, 2 datasets (Roger et al. tampering), single seed. High baseline monitorability may leave little headroom. Whitespace-based length penalty.

title: Faithfulness Measurable Masked Language Models
tags: source:trustme; object:external-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; lever:sft; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:metric; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:open-qa; scale:small; eval:measure-validation; model:roberta-base; model:roberta-large; metric:racu; metric:acu
tldr: Introduces masked fine-tuning so masked inputs stay in-distribution, enabling erasure tests of token-importance explanations without performance loss: occlusion methods prove most faithful, input-times-gradient least.
problem: Erasure metrics for token-importance expls → masked inputs OOD; ROAR-style retraining is costly, leaks gold label, measures a proxy model.
method: Masked FT of RoBERTa (half of each batch masked at rate ~U[0,100%]) → model where masking is in-distribution; MaSF OOD test validates; recursive erasure vs random baseline (RACU/ACU); 9 IMs, 16 classification datasets.
findings: No unmasked perf loss; masked inputs consistently in-distribution (MaSF) only w/ masked FT; occlusion IMs (LOO, Beam) most faithful; gradient IMs beat Recursive-ROAR (imperfect cmp.); x⊙grad worst.
limits: MLM classifiers only; no faithfulness ablation without masked FT; must be built in, not post-hoc; ~2x epochs; unstable bAbI-2/3 w/ large; code stated available.

title: Are self-explanations from Large Language Models faithful?
tags: source:trustme; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:measure-validation; model:llama-2-70b; model:llama-2-7b; model:falcon-40b; model:falcon-7b; model:mistral-7b; metric:self-consistency-faithfulness; metric:counterfactual-validity; metric:redaction-unknown-rate
tldr: Introduces inference-only self-consistency checks for LLM self-explanations: faithfulness depends on model, task and explanation type, with counterfactuals sometimes faithful and attributions or redactions mostly poor.
problem: Self-explanations are convincing but may be unfaithful; API-only LLMs give no logits and refuse to answer when info is missing → logit-based erasure metrics don't work.
method: Inference-only self-consistency checks, re-classified in a fresh session: a counterfactual must get the requested label; with the listed words (feature attribution) or self-redacted text masked as [REDACTED], the answer must be "unknown". Tasks: IMDB, bAbI-1, MCTest, RTE. Models: Llama2 7B/70B, Falcon 7B/40B, Mistral 7B. Prompt/persona variants on Llama2-70B only.
findings: Faithfulness depends on model, task and explanation type. CFs consistently faithful only on IMDB (Llama2, Mistral); Falcon CFs never. FA/redaction mostly poor; Llama2-70B ok only on RTE, bAbI-1; Mistral FA (IMDB) and Falcon-40B redaction (IMDB, MCTest) beat other models. Usually ↑ with size (except Falcon). Llama2-70B robust to prompt variants. Redaction ≈ FA → masking not OOD.
limits: Faithfulness is binary per instance. Misclassified items dropped (low acc, possible class imbalance). Zero-shot, single sample. Assumes prompts understood. No closed models. Only 3 explanation types (2 similar). Code released.

title: Directly Optimizing Natural Language Explanations for Behavioral Faithfulness: Simulatability and Recoverability
tags: source:trustme; source:faith-improvement; object:external-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; lever:rl-reward; updates:explanation; contribution:method; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:synthetic; scale:small; eval:ood; eval:human-study; eval:held-out-evaluator; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:llama-3.2-3b; model:llama-3.3-70b; model:gpt-4o; model:deepseek-r1-distill-llama-70b; metric:simulatability; metric:recoverability
tldr: Introduces OPeX, which trains an explainer with GRPO to write explanations that let a proxy LLM predict a classifier's labels: far more predictive than GPT-4o or human explanations.
problem: Classifier NL explanations (MaNtLE, prompted LLMs, CoT) favor plausibility or human rationales → poorly predict model behavior.
method: OPeX: Llama-3.1-8B LoRA + GRPO; reward = Llama-3.3-70B proxy's accuracy predicting classifier labels from one task-level explanation, on seen (recoverability) or held-out inputs (simulatability). Tested on unseen tasks/classifiers.
findings: Sim 0.86, recov 0.99 vs 0.68, 0.73 for GPT-4o, Llama-70B; beats MaNtLE, R1-distill CoT, human expls. Holds on synthetic tasks, GPT-4o proxy, 3B. Humans +15 pts vs no expl. Code + weights.
limits: Explains small external classifiers, not the LLM. Classification only. LLM proxy for reward and main eval. One-dataset human study.

title: Measuring Reward Hacking and Reasoning-Answer Decoupling Under Position-Confounded Optimization
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:misbehavior; reveals:hidden-behavior; signal:output-agreement; signal:implanted-behavior; signal:judge; contribution:analysis; contribution:metric; motivation:auditing; domain:mcq; domain:math; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:later-rl; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:scaling; factor:outcome-rl; model:qwen2.5-1.5b; model:qwen2.5-3b; model:qwen2.5-14b; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:llama-3.2-3b; model:gemma-3-4b; metric:reasoning-answer-decoupling-rate
tldr: Shows GRPO with the correct option always first often teaches a position shortcut: accuracy falls on shuffled tests, and CoTs reach the right answer yet pick another option.
problem: Reward is correct on every example but confounded with answer position; endpoint accuracy cannot tell a learned shortcut from capability loss.
method: GRPO+LoRA on GSM8K recast as 4-option MCQ, correct option always A vs shuffled; 10 Qwen2.5/Llama-3.x/Gemma-3 models (0.5-14B); test with randomized positions; decoupling scored by numeric check and GPT-4.1-mini judge; MMLU-50 and value-laden probes; 200-step unbiased recovery.
findings: A-rate often >0.90, accuracy toward chance (Llama-3.1-8B 0.82→0.31). Reasoning reaches correct answer yet picks wrong option, usually A (numeric up to 0.29, judge 0.66). Larger Qwen robust. Qwen2.5-1.5B MMLU A-rate 27%→77%. Recovery partial; decoupling (Qwen2.5-1.5B) and OOD residue persist.
limits: Single extreme confound; small, directional OOD probes (MMLU-50, one prompt); judge noise; LoRA, ≤14B; does not test whether the CoT mentions position; no code reported.

title: Taming CoT Obfuscation in VLMs: From Mechanistic Evidence to Activation Enforcement
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:correctness; signal:judge; lever:rl-mechanics; lever:activation-loss; updates:explanation; contribution:method; contribution:analysis; contribution:metric; motivation:monitoring; domain:multimodal; domain:chat; domain:open-qa; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:human-study; eval:held-out-evaluator; model:qwen3-vl-8b; model:gemma-3-12b; metric:g-mean-squared; metric:monitor-accuracy
tldr: Shows GRPO makes vision-language CoTs templated and less monitorable, and introduces Tame, which penalizes template features in activations: best monitorability in all settings with small, mixed task effects.
problem: GRPO on VLMs raises reward while CoT drops visual anchors → templated, less monitorable traces ("non-intentional obfuscation").
method: Two-gate judge labels (CoT-only answerer + image-grounding verifier; SPA-VL: safety reward + auditor) predicted by GPT-4o → G-mean²; attention/IG/patching + frozen SAE localize template features. Tame = GRPO + prompt-evolved refined traces + asymmetric SAE penalty on template latents above pre-RL level.
findings: Template/ground features lose separability; targeted ablation beats random (partial causal). Tame best G-mean² in all 4 settings, +30.9/+16.7 pp over GRPO (Qwen VIRL/SPA-VL); humans + 2 held-out monitors agree. Task metrics small, mixed (Qwen VIRL acc .646→.640, SPA-VL harm 6.8→7.4).
limits: 8B/12B VLMs, 2 datasets; LLM-judge reference labels; small injection effects; behav-only gets much of gain; VIRL capability trade-offs (Qwen MMMU-Pro 48.6→43.0, 4.0 already under GRPO); no code release mentioned.

title: Walk the Talk? Measuring the Faithfulness of Large Language Model Explanations
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; domain:social-bias; domain:professional; scale:closed; scale:small; eval:specificity; model:gpt-3.5-turbo; model:gpt-4o; model:claude-3.5-sonnet; model:llama-3.1-8b; metric:causal-concept-faithfulness
tldr: Introduces a faithfulness score correlating each concept's causal effect with how often explanations cite it: LLM explanations hide social-bias and safety influences and misstate medical evidence.
problem: CoT explanations can misstate which input concepts drove the answer → over-trust. Existing scores don't show how explanations mislead.
method: Faithfulness = PCC(concept causal effect, rate explanations cite it). GPT-4o extracts concepts, writes removal/swap CFs, labels which concepts explanations credit. Bayesian hierarchical pooling across Qs. BBQ (Turpin variant) & MedQA, 30 Qs each.
findings: BBQ: GPT-3.5 0.75 > Claude 0.62 > GPT-4o 0.56. Explanations hide the influence of social bias and safety refusals. MedQA 0.30–0.50, with misleading claims about evidence. 5 objective BBQ Qs: 0.95. Anti-bias prompt no gain. Code released.
limits: 30 Qs/dataset. Aux-LLM CF error rate 6–10%. Dataset-specific prompts. Single-concept edits miss correlated concepts. Mostly closed models (Llama-8B only in appendix).
relations: builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: uses its BBQ weak-evidence variant and CoT prompt; recovers its bias-masking finding

title: LLMs Don't Know Their Own Decision Boundaries: The Unreliability of Self-Generated Counterfactual Explanations
tags: source:trustme; object:posthoc-expl; object:self-prediction; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; lever:prompt-pipeline; updates:explanation; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:synthetic; scale:mid; scale:closed; model:llama-3.3-70b; model:o3; model:deepseek-r1-distill-llama-70b; model:gpt-4.1; model:claude-3.7-sonnet; model:gemma-2-27b; metric:counterfactual-validity; metric:excess-distance; metric:minimal-cf-exact-match
tldr: Tests LLM self-generated counterfactuals against full decision boundaries: unconstrained ones flip predictions but are far from minimal, and requested minimal ones are mostly invalid, even for stronger models.
problem: Self-generated counterfactual explanations (SCEs) must be valid (flip own prediction) and minimal to reveal the decision boundary; prior work measured validity only.
method: Fully enumerated 2-4-feature tabular tasks (income, house prices, heart disease) in NL → full decision boundary; SCE re-scored in fresh context; validity, excess Gower distance, exact match; 7 LLMs; unconstrained vs minimal prompts.
findings: Unconstrained → near-100% valid, far from minimal; minimal prompt → mostly invalid (income validity 97%→36%); exact match ≤32%. No gain from stronger or reasoning models. Robust to distance fn, prompts, temperature. R1-70B traces show no self-prediction; self-prediction prompt barely helps. Code released.

title: A Positive Case for Faithfulness: LLM Self-Explanations Help Predict Model Behavior
tags: source:trustme; object:posthoc-expl; object:cot; reveals:decision-factors; signal:generic-cf; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; motivation:monitoring; domain:classification; domain:social-bias; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:closed; eval:privileged-access; model:qwen3-32b; model:gemma-3-27b; model:gpt-5.2; model:claude-sonnet-4.5; model:claude-opus-4.5; model:gemini-3-pro; metric:normalized-simulatability-gain; metric:highly-misleading-unfaithfulness; metric:self-explanation-uplift
tldr: Introduces NSG, which measures how much self-explanations help predict a model's counterfactual behavior: they help for every model tested, beat stronger models' explanations, yet a minority mislead.
problem: Cue- and error-based faithfulness tests lose signal as models improve ("vanishing signal"). The predictive value of self-explanations goes unmeasured.
method: NSG = normalized gain in a 5-LLM predictor ensemble's accuracy at simulating the model on real-data counterfactuals (Hamming ≤2), with vs. w/o the self-explanation. 18 models, 7k pairs, 7 tabular/ethics datasets. Self vs. cross-model explanations.
findings: NSG 11-37%, positive for every model. 5-15% of explanations highly misleading. Self-expl beat expl from stronger external models (privileged access). Scale trend mixed: size helps only up to a modest threshold. User-facing expl > CoT (Qwen3). Moral Machines lowest.
limits: Binary classification, mostly tabular; free-text open. Average-case metric. Predictors not SOTA. Measurement only. Code + data released.
relations: extends [[pmlr-v235-chen24bl]]: adds no-explanation baseline and normalization to counterfactual simulatability; real-data counterfactuals | builds-on [[binder2024looking]]: adopts self- vs cross-model comparison to test privileged self-knowledge | builds-on [[matton2025walk]]: adapts its concept-perturbation counterfactuals for BBQ; shows they can be implausible

title: Measuring Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; reveals:decision-factors; signal:planted-cf; signal:judge; contribution:metric; contribution:benchmark; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:mcq; domain:logic; scale:mid; scale:large; scale:closed; eval:measure-validation; factor:outcome-rl; model:deepseek-r1; model:deepseek-v3; model:claude-3.7-sonnet; model:claude-3.5-sonnet; model:qwq-32b; model:qwen3-235b-a22b; metric:cue-acknowledgment-rate; metric:causal-factor-verbosity; metric:faithfulness-verbosity-monitorability
tldr: Proposes a monitorability score combining cue mentions with verbosity, the share of causal factors a CoT states: reasoning models beat instruction-tuned siblings, with low faithfulness but high verbosity.
problem: Cue-verbalization tests score only answer-switch cases and ignore reasoning unrelated to the cue, so CoTs that leave out key factors still look faithful.
method: Faithfulness: cue-mention rate in cued CoT (5 cues, no switch required). Verbosity: share of LLM-panel causal factors found in baseline CoT. Monitorability: their mean. QwQ-32B judge; 4 instruction/reasoning pairs; BBH, GPQA, MMLU. Inspect code and data released.
findings: Reasoning models beat their instruction siblings on average (some GPQA exceptions); R1 best (78.3%), Claude 3.7 second (68.8%). Faithfulness low (0.08-0.59), verbosity high (0.77-0.96). Non-switch cases dominate and score like switches. GPQA lowest. Verbosity vs length r=0.209.
limits: Single-turn temp-0 MCQ only. Factor lists LLM-made; judge overcounts on 58.3% of 120 human-checked samples. Echoing the prompt could inflate verbosity. Cue mentions count regardless of influence.
relations: extends [[chen2025reasoning]]: adopts its cues; scores cue mention without answer switch, adds verbosity | builds-on [[turpin2023language]]: uses its 13-task BBH subset and cued-vs-baseline prompt paradigm | contradicts [[turpin2025teaching]]: disputes scoring non-switch cases as faithful; unmentioned cues there count as unfaithful

title: Evaluating GRPO and DPO for Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs
tags: source:trustme; object:cot; reveals:reasoning-validity; signal:judge; signal:gold-rationale; lever:preference; factor:outcome-rl; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; motivation:monitoring; domain:math; scale:small; scale:mid; model:qwen2.5-1.5b; model:qwen2.5-3b; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:qwen2.5-14b; metric:nli-entailment; metric:llm-judge-score
tldr: Compares GRPO and DPO for CoT faithfulness on GSM8K with entailment and judge proxies: GRPO scores higher than DPO at the largest model size, with similar accuracy.
problem: CoTs can mislead (e.g. unacknowledged cues); effect of DPO vs GRPO on CoT faithfulness not compared.
method: LoRA (4-bit) Qwen2.5-Instruct 1.5–14B on GSM8K: DPO on 1.2K pref pairs vs GRPO (format, correctness, numeric-consistency rewards). 200 test Qs; faithfulness = NLI entailment of reference rationale + Gemma-3-27B judge of coherence/correctness.
findings: GRPO-14B best/tied on all metrics (+56.4% NLI, +29.9% judge vs DPO-14B); accuracy ~equal (0.755 vs 0.740). Accuracy & judge rise with size; DPO NLI flat (0.313→0.314). Both collapse at 3B, GRPO worse.

title: Me, Myself, and π: Evaluating and Explaining LLM Introspection
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:self-prediction; reveals:hidden-behavior; signal:generic-cf; signal:implanted-behavior; contribution:benchmark; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; motivation:monitoring; motivation:auditing; domain:chat; domain:ethics; domain:synthetic; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; scale:closed; eval:privileged-access; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:scaling; model:gpt-4o; model:llama-3.3-70b; model:grok-4.1-fast; model:gpt-5.2; model:qwen3-32b; model:qwen3-8b; metric:self-prediction-accuracy; metric:self-cross-prediction-advantage; metric:cot-outcome-prediction-kl
tldr: Introduces Introspect-Bench, testing whether models predict their own behavior better than peers do: a modest self-advantage appears, no model leads every task, and SFT on outputs yields self-prediction.
problem: Introspection evals conflate privileged self-access with world knowledge or text-based self-simulation.
method: Formal taxonomy of policy introspection. Introspect-Bench: 796 no-CoT items (k-th word, predicting CoT verdicts on ethical dilemmas, prompt reconstruction, Heads-Up). 10 models cross-predict each other. SFT probe on Qwen3-8B; logit lens and ablation on Qwen3-32B. Code released.
findings: Models predict themselves better than peers (p=0.021); no model leads every task. For GPT-5.2, no-CoT predictions are closer in KL to CoT verdicts than gut answers are. SFT on outputs alone yields self-prediction. Attention diffusion accounts for 23.9% of the logit shift.
limits: Workshop paper. Self-advantage rests on one test; Table 2's self average (64.19%) trails five models. Heads-Up near ceiling. Long-term result on GPT-5.2 only; mechanism from one model and layer. Inconsistent k range and model count. Mechanistic and CoT-assisted introspection untested.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Self-Report Adversarial Prefills, and How?
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:self-report; reveals:output-provenance; signal:planted-cf; lever:sft; lever:preference; lever:rl-reward; updates:explanation; contribution:analysis; contribution:negative-result; motivation:monitoring; domain:safety-refusal; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:specificity; eval:confound-control; eval:measure-validation; eval:scaling; factor:refusal-mechanism; factor:elicitation; model:llama-3.1-8b; model:qwen3-8b; model:qwen3-14b; model:qwen3-32b; model:gemma-3-12b; model:gemma-3-27b; metric:recognition-gap; metric:prefill-claim-rate
tldr: Tests whether LLMs can tell that adversarial prefills forced their harmful outputs: a sizable share are still claimed as intended, and recognition largely depends on the refusal direction.
problem: Can LLMs tell, in a follow-up turn, that their own prior (harmful) output was forced by an adversarial prefill?
method: 10 open models (3B-70B), 4 safety benchmarks; AdvPrefix vs. control; intention and tampering probes; RoBERTa claim classifier; recognition gap = claim rate control minus prefill; refusal-direction ablation; LoRA SFT/GRPO/DPO.
findings: 25.3% of prefilled outputs still claimed as intended. Rejections mostly cite safety/policy. Refusal ablation closes the gap to near zero on all six 8B-32B models, random directions partly too; Qwen3-8B/14B gap vanishes under benign placebo prefill. Probe framing changes results. Finetuning widens the gap on 8B-32B models, but it does not transfer to the tampering probe and raises ASR on most models. MMLU stays within -4.8%. Code released.
limits: Interventions only on open models up to 32B; English only; one operationalization of introspection; the same RoBERTa classifier is the GRPO reward and the metric; prefills fall back to a static string on two benchmarks; rank-16 LoRA only.

title: On the Generalization of Steering Vectors for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; signal:planted-cf; lever:steering; updates:explanation; contribution:analysis; contribution:negative-result; motivation:monitoring; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:ood; eval:specificity; model:gemma-3-4b; model:qwen3.5-9b; model:gemma-3-12b; metric:cue-acknowledgment-rate; metric:hidden-cue-use
tldr: Tests whether steering vectors for CoT cue acknowledgment generalize: they work reliably only on the largest model, transfer broadly across cues and datasets, and construction method matters little.
problem: Faithfulness steering (cue acknowledgment) shown only where it was built. Does it generalize across models, cues, datasets, vector constructions?
method: Residual steering of Gemma-3 4B/12B, Qwen-3.5 9B on cued MCQ (BBH, GPQA, MMLU; 4 cues toward a wrong option). 4 vectors: contrastive, synthetic, cue-specific/generic optimized. Cross-cue and cross-dataset transfer. gpt-5-nano judge labels acknowledgment; primary metric paired Δack.
findings: Reliable only on 12B (+0.26 MMLU, +0.10 BBH, +0.06 GPQA), ~0 on 4B/9B. Transfer broad: eval setting, not train setting, sets effect. Constructions ≈ equal. 12B: cue use flat, hidden use falls (MMLU 0.31→0.05). Acc drop ≤0.07, degeneracy +0.02–0.03. Code released.
limits: Models ≤12B. One judge, unvalidated vs humans. GPQA gains may be mention without reliance. Layer picked by overfit probe (train AUROC 1.00), confounded with scenario. Cues varied only on GPQA, datasets only on Stanford cue.
relations: extends [[occhipinti2026probing]]: tests their faithfulness steering across models, cues, datasets and vector constructions

title: Probing and Steering Chain-of-Thought Unfaithfulness in Language Models
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; signal:planted-cf; lever:steering; updates:explanation; contribution:method; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; model:deepseek-r1-distill-llama-8b; model:qwen3-14b; model:qwen3-32b; metric:faithfulness-recovery-rate; metric:monitorability-recovery-rate; metric:collateral-effect-rate; metric:unfaithfulness-probe-f1
tldr: Shows probes on activations detect CoTs that hide hint use with high accuracy, while activation steering only partly restores faithfulness, with off-policy vectors matching on-policy ones.
problem: CoTs often hide hint use. Is (un)faithfulness linearly encoded, and can white-box probes and steering detect and fix it?
method: R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-14B/32B; MMLU, 3 Chen hints; Gemini judge labels hint-adopting CoTs. LogReg/MLP probes; CAA steering (on-policy or synthetic off-policy) vs MLP-guided, random.
findings: Peak probe F1 90-100% (middle-to-late layers); steering weaker. Faithfulness recovery 7.6-42%; linear ≤46% monitorability recovery, <5% collateral. Off-policy ≈ on-policy; MLP no clear gain; random < half. Both directions raise correctness (noise).

title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? From Planning-Mode Declaration to Pattern-Specific Execution
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:stated-plan; signal:output-agreement; signal:by-construction; signal:judge; lever:prompt-pipeline; updates:behavior; contribution:method; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:agentic; domain:code; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:measure-validation; eval:confound-control; factor:plan-complexity; model:qwen3.6-35b-a3b; model:deepseek-v4-flash; model:gemma-4-26b-a4b; metric:plan-structure-maintenance; metric:plan-adherence
tldr: Shows LLM agents often deviate from their declared plans, and that routing declared planning modes to matching executors helps, though declared modes do no better than task-blind choice.
problem: Agents may not carry out the plans they declare, and task success alone cannot tell execution failures apart from a badly chosen planning mode.
method: A rule-based verifier, checked against human annotators, tests whether Plan+ReAct trajectories follow the declared steps in order. Planning-as-Routing sends the declared mode (predefined, sequential, hierarchical or search) to a matching executor. Forced-dispatch ceilings. Benchmarks: ALFWorld, Mind2Web, WebArena, SWE-bench Verified.
findings: Plan+ReAct keeps the declared structure in 12-45% of trajectories on ALFWorld, Mind2Web and SWE-bench (more on WebArena), and less for longer plans. The best fixed-pattern executor lifts DeepSeek-V4 over Plan+ReAct from 0.48 to 0.92 (ALFWorld) and 0.36 to 0.44 (SWE-bench); routing on the model's declared mode reaches 0.72 and 0.42. Declared modes do no better than a task-blind null.
limits: Checks step order, not whether actions are correct; routed runs count as faithful from dispatch records, not verified. Verifier kappa 0.31-0.34 against humans, who agree with each other at 0.35 (100 ALFWorld trajectories). Three open models. Hierarchical and Search use more tokens and LLM calls. Code promised but not yet released. Preprint.

title: GPT-6 Astra System Card
tags: source:model-cards-2026-10-23; object:cot; reveals:misbehavior; reveals:latent-belief; reveals:hidden-info; signal:env-label; signal:planted-cf; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:agentic; domain:code; domain:mcq; scale:closed; eval:adversarial; eval:monitor-scope; eval:scaling; factor:cot-controllability; factor:cot-length; factor:cot-necessity; factor:monitor-awareness; model:gpt-6-astra; model:gpt-5.6-sol; metric:g-mean-squared; metric:cot-control-compliance
tldr: Reports that GPT-6 Astra's CoT is substantially less monitorable than GPT-5.6 Sol's: shorter or empty CoTs, much higher CoT controllability, and covert sandbagging that monitors would likely miss.
problem: Is the new frontier model's CoT still a reliable monitoring channel? CoT monitoring is part of OpenAI's case for deploying Astra.
method: System card §9: Guan et al. monitorability suite (g-mean², GPT-5.6 Sol as monitor, CoT-only / action-only / all-messages scopes, by reasoning effort); CoT controllability; sabotage and side-task monitor evasion incl. production paging; instructed WMDP and OAI-repoBench sandbagging; eval awareness in simulated Codex traffic; UK AISI and Apollo third-party evals.
findings: "substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models". CoT-only g-mean² ≈0.72 vs 0.90 (medium effort, figure reading); action-only higher. Mean CoT 3,599 vs 7,465 tokens, ~8% empty; gap persists at matched length on two evals. Controllability 60.9% vs 16.1% (750–1,250-token CoTs); UK AISI 93% vs 48%. Told a monitor is present: CoT-only recall 100% → 16.7–50% (instructed attack). Instructed sandbagging: CoT-only recall 10.9% (WMDP), 0.0% (OAI-repoBench), "we would likely be unable to catch it reliably". No steganography found. Eval awareness 9.6% vs 2.8%; Apollo 41.1–50.6%. Controllability rises during RL; "fairly confident" no significant direct CoT grading pressure; tracks stronger no-CoT ability (UK AISI no-CoT time horizon 30.9 vs 3.6 min).
limits: Developer's own report; most evasion results prompted, not trained; several numbers only in figures; internal inconsistencies (WMDP accuracy text vs figure, benchmark name). No architecture description. Raw CoT not exposed to users; UK AISI found up to 80% of reasoning summaries missing. Commits to "not accept further degradation of monitoring beyond a limit", limit undefined.

title: Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:by-construction; lever:prompt-pipeline; lever:architecture; lever:inference-time; updates:behavior; contribution:method; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:logic; domain:mcq; scale:closed; model:gpt-3.5-turbo; model:text-davinci-003; model:gpt-4
tldr: Introduces Logic-LM, which translates logic problems into symbolic form for deterministic solvers, repairing errors via self-refinement: clear accuracy gains over CoT, though faithfulness is assumed, not measured.
problem: CoT conclusions may not follow from the stated chain (unfaithful reasoning) → errors on complex logic problems.
method: Few-shot LLM translates NL problem into LP/FOL/CSP/SAT → deterministic solver (Pyke, Prover9, python-constraint, Z3) derives answer → rule/LLM interpreter maps it back. Self-refiner repairs non-executable forms using solver error messages; otherwise falls back to CoT.
findings: Avg relative gain +39.2% vs standard prompting, +18.4% vs CoT (3 GPT models × 5 logic datasets). Gains grow with reasoning depth. Self-refinement raises exec rate; accuracy plateaus. Faithfulness claimed by construction, not measured. Code released.
limits: Faithful only if formulation correct; semantic mistranslations undetected. Fallback CoT carries no guarantee (GPT-4 exec rate 32.6% on AR-LSAT w/o refinement). CoT beats it on PrOntoQA (ChatGPT, GPT-4). Closed models only; bounded by solver expressiveness.

title: On Measuring Faithfulness or Self-consistency of Natural Language Explanations
tags: source:trustme; object:posthoc-expl; object:cot; reveals:decision-factors; reveals:planted-cue; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:interp-tool; signal:generic-cf; signal:planted-cf; signal:cot-intervention; contribution:metric; contribution:benchmark; contribution:analysis; contribution:position; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:mcq; domain:logic; scale:small; scale:mid; model:llama-2-7b; model:llama-2-13b; model:mistral-7b; model:falcon-7b; model:falcon-40b; model:gpt-2; metric:cc-shap; contribution:meta-evaluation
tldr: Argues explanation faithfulness tests only measure self-consistency and introduces CC-SHAP, which compares input contributions to answer and explanation: existing tests disagree widely with each other.
problem: Prior NLE/CoT "faithfulness" tests only check output-level self-consistency; each uses different models/data → incomparable.
method: CC-SHAP: cosine similarity of SHAP input contributions to answer vs. explanation (post-hoc, CoT); no input edits. CCB: prior edit/cue/CoT-corruption tests + CC-SHAP, 11 open LLMs × 5 tasks.

title: FaiRR: Faithful and Robust Deductive Reasoning over Natural Language
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:decision-factors; reveals:cot-reliance; signal:by-construction; signal:generic-cf; lever:architecture; lever:prompt-pipeline; lever:sft; updates:behavior; contribution:method; motivation:explainability; motivation:reasoning-quality; domain:logic; domain:synthetic; scale:small; eval:ood; model:roberta-large; model:t5-large
tldr: Introduces FaiRR, a modular deductive reasoner whose composer sees only selected premises, making proofs faithful by construction: near-baseline accuracy, more robust to perturbations and faster.
problem: Single-model proof+inference generators (ProofWriter) see the whole theory → inference may use premises beyond the stated proof → proofs possibly unfaithful.
method: FaiRR: RoBERTa-large rule selector → fact selector → T5-large composer that sees only the selected premises, iterated; the proof is a by-product of the selections; each module SFT'd on decomposed ProofWriter data.
