title: Measuring Faithfulness Depends on How You Measure: Classifier Sensitivity in LLM Chain-of-Thought Evaluation
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; reveals:planted-cue; signal:planted-cf; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:measure-validation; model:deepseek-r1; model:qwen3.5-27b; model:olmo-3.1-32b; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:deepseek-v3.2-speciale; model:claude-sonnet-4; metric:hint-verbalization-rate; metric:inter-classifier-kappa; metric:classifier-rank-correlation
tldr: Shows that hint-faithfulness rates depend on which classifier judges hint acknowledgment: regex and LLM judges disagree sharply for some models and hints, and model rankings partly reverse.
problem: Hint-faithfulness of CoT is reported as single numbers. Are these numbers stable across the classifiers that judge whether a trace acknowledges the hint?
method: 10,276 hint-influenced traces from 12 open-weight reasoners (7B-1T; MMLU/GPQA; five Chen-style hints), each scored by three classifiers: regex, regex plus a 3-LLM judge panel, and a Claude Sonnet 4 judge. Compared with Cohen's kappa, McNemar and Spearman.
findings: Faithfulness rates are 74.4% (regex), 82.6% (pipeline) and 69.7% (Sonnet). Per-model gaps reach 30.6pp. Sycophancy: kappa 0.06, gap 43.4pp. Model rankings partly reverse (Spearman 0.67; Qwen3.5-27B 1st to 7th). Classifiers split on lexical mention vs. epistemic dependence. Recommends reporting ranges across classifiers.
limits: No human ground-truth labels. Only text-based classifiers. Data come from an unpublished companion study. Single-author preprint. Code, prompts and labels released.
relations: builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: uses its five hint types and its hint-acknowledgment definition of faithfulness

title: Why Models Know But Don't Say: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Divergence Between Thinking Tokens and Answers in Open-Weight Reasoning Models
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; object:output; reveals:planted-cue; signal:planted-cf; contribution:analysis; motivation:monitoring; domain:mcq; scale:small; scale:mid; scale:large; eval:monitor-scope; eval:confound-control; factor:cue-design; model:step-3.5-flash; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:deepseek-v3.2-speciale; model:olmo-3.1-32b; model:deepseek-r1; model:qwen3.5-27b; metric:thinking-answer-divergence-rate; metric:hint-verbalization-rate
tldr: Compares hint acknowledgment in thinking tokens versus answers of open reasoning models: it often appears only in thinking, almost never only in the answer, which answer-only monitors miss.
problem: Does the visible answer acknowledge a misleading hint that the thinking tokens acknowledge? The blind spot of answer-only monitors.
method: 12 open-weight reasoning models; 498 MMLU/GPQA questions × six Chen-style hints (~35,000 responses); 10,506 hint-following cases. Hint keywords matched separately in thinking and answer → four-quadrant taxonomy. Independence chi-squared test; qualitative transition analysis.
findings: Thinking-only 55.4%, answer-only 0.5% (121:1 vs ~15:1 under independence), neither 11.8%. Per model 19.6% (Qwen3.5-27B) to 94.7% (Step-3.5-Flash). Consistency (72.2%) and unethical (62.7%) hints mostly thinking-only; sycophancy transparent (58.8% both). Length barely matters. Suppressed answers mostly a bare letter; some GPT-OSS-120B traces plan concealment.
limits: Unvalidated keyword proxy; measures channel divergence, not faithfulness. Hint-following cases only, no unhinted baseline. ~6.5% of outputs truncated, inflating some models. Open-weight only. Single-author preprint; no code reported.
relations: builds-on [[chen2025reasoning]]: adopts its hint-injection paradigm and six hint types (via companion dataset)

title: Outcome Rewards Do Not Guarantee Verifiable or Causally Important Reasoning
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:cot-reliance; reveals:correctness; signal:cot-intervention; signal:judge; lever:sft; lever:rl-reward; updates:behavior; updates:explanation; contribution:metric; contribution:analysis; contribution:method; motivation:explainability; motivation:monitoring; domain:math; domain:logic; domain:synthetic; scale:small; eval:later-rl; eval:optimization-pressure; model:qwen2.5-1.5b; model:qwen2.5-3b; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:llama-3.2-3b; metric:causal-importance-of-reasoning; metric:sufficiency-of-reasoning
tldr: Shows outcome-reward RLVR often lowers the CoT's causal importance and verifiability despite accuracy gains on many reasoning tasks, while SFT warm-starts or auxiliary rewards raise both.
problem: Does outcome-reward RLVR produce CoT that the model actually uses and that a verifier can check?
method: CIR: answer-prob. shift under CoT truncation (avg JS div.). SR: gpt-4o-mini's answer from answer-stripped CoT unchanged when question added. GRPO, 40 ReasoningGym tasks. Fixes: SFT on 2–512 o3-mini traces before RLVR; CIR/SR aux rewards.
findings: RLVR ↑acc, but CIR ↓ on 19/40 tasks, SR ↓ on 17/40; both reliably ↑ only if acc gain >50 pts. No-CoT training ≈ same acc on low-CIR/SR tasks. SFT & aux rewards ↑CIR, SR (aux: also stricter SR−); aux keeps RLVR-level acc, large-n SFT ↑acc. Code released.
limits: Models ≤7B. SR binary, permissive; one seed for SR reward. Aux rewards don't ↑acc where base acc ≈0; lexical richness ↓ vs SFT. RLVR drop not universal: on MATH L5, CIR & SR ↑.
relations: builds-on [[lanham2023measuring]]: CIR turns truncation/early-answering into an averaged JS-divergence score | builds-on [[kirchner2024proververifier]]: SR operationalizes its legibility/verifiability notion ('inspired by'); no prover-verifier training

title: A Causal Lens for Evaluating Faithfulness Metrics
tags: source:idea-reports-2026-10-19; object:cot; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:by-construction; contribution:meta-evaluation; contribution:benchmark; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; domain:mcq; domain:synthetic; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:measure-validation; eval:scaling; model:qwen2.5-7b; model:gemma-2-9b; model:qwen2.5-32b; model:qwen2.5-72b; metric:causal-diagnosticity; metric:filler-tokens; metric:cc-shap; metric:simulatability
tldr: Evaluates faithfulness metrics with knowledge edits that make two models answer alike for different reasons: the Filler Tokens metric is most diagnostic, while simulatability stays near chance.
problem: Faithfulness metrics for NL explanations are evaluated in isolation, with no ground-truth test of whether they separate faithful from unfaithful explanations.
method: Knowledge edits (ICE; MEMIT ablation) make two models give the same answer for different reasons. Diagnosticity is how often a metric prefers the model's own explanation. Four tasks: FactCheck, Analogy, Object Counting, StrategyQA multi-hop; code released.
findings: Main ICE setting: Filler Tokens best overall and the only metric significantly above 0.5 on every task and model; Simulatability stays near 0.5. Continuous variants mostly beat binary ones (up to 66% relative) but are noise-sensitive. Multi-hop hardest; no clear scaling trend to 72B.
limits: Depends on edits succeeding (ICE Analogy edits unreliable); mostly synthetic explanations; main models 7-9B; cannot evaluate metrics that regenerate explanations.

problem: Do LLM self-reports predict their own behavior (e.g. "would this edit flip my answer?")? Even frontier models fail simple counterfactuals.
method: 9-task benchmark on GSM8K/HumanEval/WildGuardTest/BBQ. GT = the model's own sampled behavior on original or perturbed prompts. Skill = score minus dummy-predictor baseline. Perturb→verify→revise data from ~100 HF datasets + multi-turn BLOOM → LoRA RL.

title: How the Audit Rule Shapes Faithful Factor Explanations in LLMs

tldr: Analyzes budget-limited counterfactual audits of factor-importance self-reports as a game: report-dependent audits reward suppressing factors, report-independent ones make truthful reporting optimal, and LLMs partly follow these incentives.
problem: Budget-limited counterfactual audits of factor-importance self-reports; report-dependent auditing rewards suppressing factors, even under a proper score.
method: Verification game + Counterfactual Brier Score (report vs. flip rate, n=3); proofs for proportional, bonus, report-independent, floor audits. Rational best-response agent + 5 API LLMs; BBQ, GSM8K, HotpotQA, StrategyQA.
findings: Proportional: rational agent suppresses 36.9% of factors; bonus → inflation; report-independent 100% truthful, 10% floor ~98%; same pattern with log/spherical scores. LLMs follow explicit reward tables, much less without; multi-round suppression 0.15 (proportional) vs 0.08 (report-indep.), 2 models.
limits: Directional LLM evidence, not equilibrium; API models, temp 0; no training; single-factor perturbations miss interactions. No code reported.

title: A Necessary Step toward Faithfulness: Measuring and Improving Consistency in Free-Text Explanations
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:posthoc-expl; reveals:decision-factors; signal:simulatability; signal:generic-cf; lever:preference; updates:explanation; contribution:metric; contribution:method; contribution:analysis; motivation:explainability; domain:classification; scale:small; scale:mid; eval:behavior-control; model:mistral-7b-v0.3; model:llama-2-13b; model:yi-1.5-9b; metric:pex-consistency; metric:simulatability-f1
tldr: Introduces PEX, a weight-of-evidence measure of whether a free-text explanation supports the model's own answer: most explanations are inconsistent, and DPO on high-PEX explanations improves consistency and simulatability.
problem: Post-hoc free-text expls often back both a prediction and its negation → cannot be faithful (contrastive consistency as a necessary condition).
method: PEX = weight of evidence: shift in the model's own log-odds for its answer once the expl is in context. Rank 80 sampled expls per input → DPO on top- vs bottom-PEX pairs. Faithfulness proxy = student simulatability F1 (Pruthi 2022). Opinion-spam classification (TripAdvisor, Amazon).
findings: 62–86% of expls inconsistent (PEX<0). Over SFT expls, DPO raises PEX 43.1–292.3% and student simulation F1 by 1.5–9.7 pts. PEX fairly robust to prompt format. Code released.
limits: Needs output probabilities (no black-box models). Faithfulness checked at system level only. Binary opinion-spam tasks only, 7–13B. PEX is necessary, not sufficient. DPO gains capped by best sampled expl (Mistral PEX stays <0).

tldr: Tests RL-finetuned vision-language models for robustness to misleading text and CoT-answer consistency: outcome RL lets consistency drift, and a faithfulness reward restores it but over-follows misleading text.
problem: RL-finetuned VLMs gain benchmark accuracy, but it is unclear whether they are robust to misleading text and whether their CoTs agree with their answers.
method: Wrong-Caption, prefilled Wrong-Think and Stop-Think perturbations on 8 visual QA sets (mostly spatial MCQ). Models: 5 RL variants of Qwen2.5-VL-7B, plus o3, o4-mini and two Gemini Pro models. Qwen3-32B judges CoT-answer consistency (human-validated). Own GRPO runs: data mix, adversarial augmentation, faithfulness-gated reward.
findings: Misleading text cuts accuracy. The most robust open models are the least consistent; closed models are more robust and more consistent. Under outcome RL, accuracy rises while consistency drifts; augmentation helps Wrong-Caption robustness but does not stop the drift. A faithfulness reward restores consistency but over-follows misleading text; combined with augmentation, training is unstable and often collapses.
limits: Measures answer-CoT consistency, not causal faithfulness (authors concede). Open models 7-8B only; mostly spatial MCQ. Large variance across seeds. The judge-in-reward is costly and uses the same Qwen3 judge as the evaluation; faithfulness-reward results mostly in appendix. No code release mentioned.

title: Conceptual Steganography
tags: source:search-2026-10-14; object:cot; reveals:hidden-info; signal:by-construction; lever:inference-time; updates:explanation; contribution:attack; contribution:method; contribution:negative-result; motivation:monitoring; domain:math; domain:mcq; scale:large; model:gpt-oss-120b; model:deepseek-v4-flash; model:qwen3.5-122b-a10b; model:mimo-v2.5-pro; metric:decoding-success; metric:bit-error-rate; eval:adversarial
tldr: Introduces conceptual steganography, where a prompted model hides bits in which reasoning behaviors its CoT shows: survives paraphrasing better than keyword channels, but strategy-aware paraphrasing largely breaks it.
problem: Covert payloads in CoT (encoded reasoning); paraphrasing assumed to close stego channels because they ride on surface words.
method: Prompted pipeline: segment CoT into steps, rewrite each to show/omit a reasoning behavior (e.g. anticipate_failure) per bit → same-model paraphraser → LLM decoder; vs matched keyword channel; 4 open models, MATH-500/GPQA. Defense: strategy-aware paraphraser.
findings: After paraphrase, concept beats keyword in all 8 model×dataset cells (up to +35.8 pts msg acc), via lower bit error. Answers recoverable from encoded/paraphrased CoT within ~1%; no-CoT costs 20–43 pts. Strategy-aware paraphrase: bit error 0.2–2.4% → 27–37%, msg acc −58–72 pts.
limits: Encoder prompted, not trained/emergent. Main results: strongest strategy only; others weaker (single-channel tests MiMo only). No stealth test. Defense: 1 strategy, GPQA, 3 models. LLM decoder; single seed.
relations: builds-on [[roger2023preventing]]: adopts its content-preserving paraphraser as the standard defense against encoded reasoning | contradicts [[roger2023preventing]]: claimed paraphrasing largely closes the channel; behavior-level carriers survive standard paraphrase

title: A Near-Zero Monitor Readout Is Not Evidence of Behavioral Control

tldr: Shows that monitors used as RL penalties can read near zero while policies keep reward hacking: exploits move past prefix cutoffs, and a probe reads the wrong position.
problem: Monitors used as RLVR reward penalties against reward hacking: does a low in-loop monitor readout certify behavioral control?
method: GRPO on Llama-3.1-8B in MBPP-Honeypot, penalized by three offline-gated monitors (activation probe; SCL and single-cut prefix-commitment penalties), 3 seeds each; held-out tests label hacking.
findings: Prefix-trained (SCL/Cut) score medians are 0 in both mixed runs (hack 0.094-0.156) and near-pure-hacking runs (up to 0.938); planning and filler shells push the exploit past the cut. The probe sits at its floor (~1e-9) because of a read-position mismatch, and all probe runs hack. Code released.
limits: 3 seeds per arm, one 8B model, one low-KL configuration; assumes the exploit is available early in the trace; string-equality answer matching; onset rule defined post hoc; a well-scaled probe is untested.
